#3560. 50 Years Later, Rocky's Best Line Is Still The Greatest Underdog Quote In Movie History

When we use the phrase "cinematic classic," there are some pretty universal movies that are likely to flash through one's mind. "The Godfather." "The Shawshank Redemption." "Psycho." "The Wizard of Oz." But undoubtedly amongst those all-time great titles is also "Rocky," the underdog story for the ages that made Sylvester Stallone a star.

The reception to "Rocky" upon release was a surprise for everyone involved. Not only was it a huge commercial hit, but it also went on to win Best Picture at the Oscars, with John G. Avildsen also winning Best Director. Not bad for a movie written and starring a guy nobody had really heard of before 1976.

Beyond the accolades though, 50 years later, "Rocky" is still so much more than a boxing movie. It's a remarkably crafted rags to riches story with a stellar performance by Stallone. It contains one of the best fights ever and the greatest training montage of all time. It also paved the way for a long-running, shockingly enduring franchise that led to some other great movies, including "Creed," which earned Stallone a Best Supporting Actor Oscar nomination decades after he first put on the gloves as Rocky Balboa.

For all of the movie's memorable moments and for all of its quotable lines, one quote sums up its underdog premise better than any other.

"All I wanna do is go the distance. Nobody's ever gone the distance with Creed, and if I can go that distance, you see, and that bell rings and I'm still standin', I'm gonna know for the first time in my life, see, that I weren't just another bum from the neighborhood." – Rocky Balboa

This quote really sums up the mission statement of the first "Rocky" movie in a nutshell. It's a true underdog story, right up until the end. It wasn't ever about him winning. This is a man who had nothing, felt like nothing, and was very unhappy with life as it existed. Given the opportunity, he made the very most of it and proved what he needed to prove to the world yes but, more importantly, to himself.

The ending of "Rocky" proves that he's not just another bum from the neighborhood. Win, lose, or draw, he went the distance with Apollo Creed, which made him a winner in a more meaningful way than winning any single boxing match. It's more about the journey than the destination. It's easy to be concerned about winning or achieving some goal that we believe might finally fix that hole deep inside of us but Rocky Balboa, with this quote, demonstrates a timeless understanding of what really matters.

Winning is great, but winning can take many forms. Rocky didn't defeat Creed but he won. He won a sense of purpose. He won a life he enjoyed. He won Adrian. He won in a far more meaningful way. This quote, once the movie's ending hits, rings loud and carries a lot of emotional weight.

"You're gonna eat lightnin' and you're gonna crap thunder!"

"My old man, he was never too smart. He says to me, 'You weren't born with much of a brain, so you better start using your body.' So I become a fighter."

"Forget about sports as a profession. Sports make ya grunt and smell. See, be a thinker, not a stinker."

"I been coming here for six years, and for six years ya been sticking it to me, and I wanna know how come!"

"Apollo Creed vs. the Italian Stallion. Sounds like a damn monster movie!"

When Calls the Heart’s 13th season ended with a proposal amid the 2026 TV schedule, and fan have since been clamoring for more! Fan-favorite couple Elizabeth Thornton (Erin Krakow) and Nathan Grant (Kevin McGarry) finally got engaged on the long-running Hallmark drama, and Hope Valley is abuzz with wedding preparations. As filming for Season 14 begins to wrap up, the network has released a new look, and Hearties have a lot of thoughts in the aftermath of that wedding-centric trailer.

Just recently, Hallmark Channel surprised fans by releasing a new trailer for WCTH Season 14, which officially premieres this coming January. Naturally, the trailer centers on Elizabeth and Nathan’s much-anticipated nuptials, and how the town is preparing. The two characters seem to be content about their impending union couple, and the excitement is definitely building in Hope Valley:

A post shared by Hallmark Channel (@hallmarkchannel)

Elizabeth and Nathan’s engagement and subsequent wedding have been a long time coming. Viewers have witnessed quite a bit on the romance front, including the love triangle between Elizabeth, Nathan and Lucas (Chris McNally). The two have gone through a lot together and separately, and as someone who has been rooting for them for a while, I could not be happier that this is finally happening. And I’m not the only one. Plenty of Hearties took to the comments of the Instagram video to share their excitement, including user apeyberg, who loves this early Christmas present:

❤️ Oh. My. Goodness! Can't wait! Thank you so much Hallmark Channel! The BEST Christmas gift!

Given filming on When Calls the Heart's new season is nearly done and the show usually returns pretty early in a given year, this trailer being dropped now makes sense. Like the fan above, I am definitely happy about this early present, and it’s just what fans need to get them hyped about what's to come. However, now that the first trailer is out and we've seen glimpses of what's to come, the wait could become even more tougher. Still, pcmy01’s excitement is building:

The anticipation and excitement that’s building up inside ALL WCTH FANS right now is skyrocketing!!! I, we, can hardly hold it together. This is gonna be epic! 🙌🏾♥️🤩🔥🔥🔥🔥🔥

Ever since the Season 13 finale aired in March, I've personally found the wait for Season 14 to be tough, and I'm not sure this great new tease is going to make that easier for me. Nevertheless, it's evident that ahead of Thanksgiving, fans are just thankful to have any kind taste of the new episodes. And, based on the comment shared by heartiefollower, this little promo is going to go a long way amid the wait:

I'm so glad this promo lasts for 20 minutes 😍

Meanwhile, along with Nathan and Elizabeth’s wedding, there is something else that fans can look forward to. Season 14 will mark the return of Lori Loughlin’s Abigail Stanton. It was announced last year that the Full House alum would be back in after exiting the show during Season 6. Fans got a glimpse of Abigail at the very end of the Season 13 finale when she officially returned to Hope Valley, and loriloughlinerinkrakowfan is excited to have her back:

So BEYOND happy to have our Abigail back!!! 🥹💕

There is indeed a lot to be excited about for When Calls the Heart Season 14. And, aside from the wedding and Loughlin’s much-celebrated return, I can imagine the producers having more surprises in store, and Hearties seem as anxious as ever. The reveal of the premiere date also makes the prospect of the show's return feel much more real. mamazach_jackiez is looking forward to everything coming in Season 14, and I’m right there with them:

I can barely wait, so looking forward to this beautiful wedding and all season 14 brings!

Like so many others, I really hope the wait for When Calls the Heart's return won't be too bad. Hopefully, now that we’re getting into the holiday season, time will be moving a little bit quicker. That aside, though, I'm optimistic that the moment Nathan and Elizabeth finally say “I do” will be well worth the wait. On that note, WCTH Season 14 premieres on Sunday, January 3 at 8 p.m. ET on Hallmark Channel.

#3558. Why Kate Middleton's Return to William's Side Says a Lot About the Future of the Monarchy

After days of rumors circulating about Kate Middleton’s possible participation in the trip to India, confirmation came only at the last minute. This news came as a surprise in many ways, even though the princess’s presence was expected. Her involvement in this tour of India deserves attention, especially in light of the increasingly important role she plays alongside Prince William, who will be king. The trip to India, significant in its own right, also included an important meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, aimed at strengthening relations between the United Kingdom and India. This high-profile diplomatic meeting was added after it was confirmed that Modi would return in time from his trip to the Philippines.

The Prince and Princess of Wales arrive at the Earthshot ceremony

Kate’s participation in the royal tour was made official by Kensington Palace only the day before departure to allow the princess to assess her condition right up until the last minute and determine whether she could handle such a demanding trip, following her recovery. But once she arrived in Mumbai, Catherine proved she was ready to do more than initially planned. The princess appeared, as always, impeccable and smiling—perhaps even more so than usual—in her customary understated and polished style. She greeted the crowd and met with people who had come to see her, participating in events alongside her husband.

From the first day of this three-day tour—which began on the anniversary of their official engagement— Kate immediately displayed her characteristic good-natured spirit, evident in past tours as well, by joining Prince William in a game of gully cricket—a street version of the sport—alongside local children and teenagers. Serving as host was Sachin Tendulkar, an Indian sports legend whom the couple had already met during their previous visit to the country in 2016. The two princes put their skills to the test with little formality. They then took a ride on the Mumbai metro—a scene we’d already seen in London in candid photos when the Princess of Wales traveled on a bus in celebration of London Poppy Day.

The Princess of Wales at the awards ceremony

The highlight was the awards ceremony in Mumbai on the evening of the second day, when the Princess of Wales unexpectedly took the stage to deliver a speech dedicated to the power of nature, health, and healing. Her speech was kept secret until the last moment, so much so that not even the celebrities and other guests in attendance knew the Princess of Wales would be speaking. “Nature is precious,” the princess said. “We are not separate from it. We are part of it, deeply connected in ways both visible and unseen…the health of the planet and our natural world is inseparable from our own, and when it thrives, so do we,” she continued. “I have seen firsthand how nature has the power to heal and enrich our daily lives, but so much remains under threat.” “There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time."

Catherine then presented the award in the “Protect and Restore Nature” category, dedicated to the protection and restoration of ecosystems. “The people we’re celebrating tonight are a huge part of that story. Their work will inspire and create seismic change that will improve lives for generations to come,” she said.

The Prince and Princess of Wales at the awards ceremony

Over the past three days, William and Kate have been busy meeting about sustainability, innovation, transportation, culture, and relations between the two countries. William is, in fact, assuming an increasingly prominent role on the international stage, supporting the United Kingdom’s diplomatic relations through his travels, which Middleton’s presence reinforced. This time, however, it was not simply a princess accompanying her husband on an official visit, but a woman who, after her illness and a long hiatus from major trips abroad, chose to return to her rightful role—and one the public has long expected her to fill.

The Prince and Princess of Wales with some Earthshot Prize winners

It’s worth noting that this is the first time in four years—since her illness—that Kate has accompanied Prince William on an official overseas mission. The last such occasion was in December 2022, when the couple traveled to Boston, Massachusetts, for the Earthshot Prize ceremony. Her participation in the trip to India thus reflects her desire to gradually resume her international role, as well as her awareness of just how important her presence is to the monarchy.

After her cancer diagnosis in 2024, Catherine prioritized her health and family, returning to public engagements without rushing things. However, her trip to Reggio Emilia, Italy, last May marked an important first step. On that occasion, she appeared visibly engaged and enthusiastic, and in subsequent statements, she hinted at her desire to travel more and gradually resume international engagements. “So I’m so glad it went well for her. I think she came back buzzing.” William said, describing his wife’s mood after that trip. Court circles had also hinted that Catherine wished to gradually resume a more active schedule.

The Prince and Princess of Wales at the 2026 Earthshot Prize ceremony

Her return to work, however, was approached gradually, respecting the time needed for her recovery. It’s a journey that Kate herself described with great sincerity in a recent interview published last week in Country Life, a magazine for which Prince William served as guest editor. “I was told in hospital that my recovery would not be linear. There will be good days and bad days, that it will take time,” the princess said, emphasizing that recovery does not necessarily proceed in a steady and predictable manner. India, therefore, did not come as a complete surprise. Rather, it was the realization of a desire that Middleton had already begun to express, and that the princess agreed to undertake such a demanding trip shows she felt ready to take the next step.

The Prince and Princess of Wales in India

Before the trip, Kensington Palace issued a statement emphasizing how much the princess cares about her husband’s environmental initiative and how meaningful it was for her to return to participate in the ceremony in person. “She’s enormously proud of what he’s achieved, and it has been particularly special for them to experience this moment together. They are very much a team.”

This refers to the project’s growth; since her last participation in Boston in 2022, it has significantly expanded its international reach and the impact of the initiatives it supports. “This year’s program in Mumbai promises to be the biggest and most ambitious yet, and she’s excited to see first-hand just how far some of it has come and meet some of the extraordinary people behind that success.” The spokesperson then recalled the couple’s previous trip to India in 2016, explaining that both have particularly fond memories of that visit. “The prince and princess are both really looking forward to what promises to be a fantastic week in India. They have such fond memories of their last visit together in 2016, and are excited to be returning a decade later.”

As mentioned, the most important diplomatic event of the tour took place on November 18 in New Delhi, where Prince William and Kate met with Prime Minister Narendra Modi. This was the only occasion during the visit when the royal couple left Mumbai, the city that hosted most of their scheduled engagements. Modi returned to the Indian capital specifically for this occasion after attending a major international summit in Manila, Philippines, to take part in the bilateral talks.

A spokesperson for Kensington Palace had emphasized the strategic importance of relations between the two countries, characterized by deep and ever-growing ties in numerous sectors, which include trade, investment, defense, security, technology, education, and culture. Kate’s presence alongside William during the meeting was considered particularly significant. “This meeting reflects the importance of that relationship, as well as the role their royal highnesses can play in celebrating and strengthening the ties between our two countries.”

“For the prince, it also represents another significant engagement as he continues to take on a growing role on the international stage. We’ve seen him increasingly support the UK’s diplomatic relationships through his overseas engagements, and this meeting will provide an opportunity to build on those connections at the highest level.”

India, after all, holds a special place in the history of relations between the British monarchy and the Commonwealth. King Charles has visited the country numerous times, on both official and private occasions, strengthening a personal and institutional relationship over the years. For William and Catherine, however, this trip represented an opportunity to build a direct relationship with a nation destined to play an increasingly important role in the international balance of power.

A close-up of the Prince and Princess of Wales

With a population of over 1.4 billion people, India is now the world’s most populous country and one of the fastest-growing economies. Hosting the Earthshot Prize meant engaging a potentially massive audience on issues of environmental sustainability, resource conservation, and innovative solutions to combat climate change.

A beautiful image of the Prince and Princess of Wales

For William and Kate, returning to India also meant revisiting a country to which they are bound by personal memories. As mentioned, their last visit was in April 2016, when the Prince and Princess of Wales—then the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge—undertook an official tour of India and Bhutan at the request of the British government. During that trip, they visited Mumbai, met with representatives from India’s cultural and sports communities, and traveled to Agra, where they admired the Taj Mahal.

Right in front of the famous mausoleum—a symbol of eternal love—William and Kate sat on the same white marble bench where, 24 years earlier, Lady Diana, Princess of Wales, posed during a visit to India. That photograph of Diana, portrayed alone in front of the monument, became one of the most iconic images of her public life. Taken in 1992, when her marriage to Charles was going through a deep crisis, many interpreted it as a visual representation of her loneliness. In 2016, William and Kate’s decision to recreate that shot inevitably brought Diana to mind, adding a personal and symbolic dimension to their visit.

For Catherine, therefore, this trip is above all a new step on her journey back to public life following her illness. Not a demonstration of recovery to be celebrated as a race against time, but an opportunity to resume playing an important role while moving at her own pace. And to stand once again alongside William on a mission that concerns not only the future of the monarchy, but also that of the planet.

Originally published by Vanity Fair Italy.

#3557. Why Effie Trinket From The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Looks So Familiar

Effie Trinket, the character played by Elizabeth Banks in the original set of "Hunger Games" movies, is a larger-than-life, ridiculous, and flamboyant woman initially concerned with appearance above all else — even though her job is to beautify and briefly pamper impoverished children before they head to their deaths. It's hard to imagine this character, who appears in "The Hunger Games," "Catching Fire," and both parts of the adaptation of the book "Mockingjay," being played by anybody but Banks, yet the newest addition to the "Hunger Games" universe, the film version of "Sunrise on the Reaping," features a younger iteration of Effie. So, who brings her to life, and what role does Effie play in this prequel?

Suzanne Collins released the novel "Sunrise on the Reaping" in 2025, and before the book even hit shelves, a film adaptation (with the expanded title "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping") was in the works. Ultimately, Joseph Zada was cast as a young Haymitch Abernathy, the character made famous by Woody Harrelson alongside Banks in the first four "Hunger Games" movies. A ton of huge names, including Kieran Culkin, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, and Ralph Fiennes, went on to join the movie's cast from there, with Elle Fanning being recruited to fill Banks' sky-high pastel shoes and play Effie as well.

We see Effie in "Sunrise on the Reaping" as a fledgling stylist desperate to prove herself ... and not only does she end up styling Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes when a senior stylist falls through, but she provides emotional support to Haymitch before and after he wins the Games. But where have you seen Fanning before? Plenty of places.

If the last name "Fanning" just looks familiar from the outset, that's because Elle Fanning and her older sister Dakota Fanning have been performing since they were kids. In fact, the younger Fanning played a younger version of her sister while making her film debut in "I Am Sam" in 2001.

From there, Elle Fanning showed up in family-friendly fare like "Daddy Day Care" and "Because of Winn-Dixie" (as well as considerably more adult films like "Babel"), but the fact of the matter is that Fanning essentially grew up on-screen. Both Fanning sisters navigated their journeys from child stars to adult actors in pretty incredible ways, but we're talking about Elle Fanning here, and her career does stand on its own. After playing younger roles in "Super 8," "We Bought a Zoo," and "Maleficent," she moved into more firmly adult parts in the films "The Neon Demon," "20th Century Women," "The Beguiled," and "Mary Shelley," just to name a few.

Without question, Fanning's most visible big-screen appearances aside from "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" have recently come in "A Complete Unknown," "Predator: Badlands," and "Sentimental Value." In "A Complete Unknown," she plays Sylvie Russo, the girlfriend to Timothée Chalamet's Bob Dylan and a character who's loosely based on Dylan's real girlfriend Suze Rotolo. In "Predator: Badlands," Fanning plays the protagonist Thia and her evil twin sister Tessa and was able to use her own odd physicality for the role. As for "Sentimental Value," Joachim Trier's gorgeous family drama earned Fanning her first Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress at the 2026 ceremony.

Remarkably, Elle Fanning's small-screen career is just as robust as her big-screen one — and she's earned almost as much acclaim to boot. I personally remember seeing the younger Fanning as early as 2006 in the particularly depraved "Law & Order: Special Victims Unit" episode "Cage" (fans of that show know exactly which one I'm talking about), but 2020 marked her big TV break with "The Great," a truly great — pun intended! — historical drama that casts Fanning as Catherine the Great. In this deliberately anachronistic, deeply funny, and exceptionally bawdy series created by "The Favourite" screenwriter Tony McNamara, Fanning gets to play the future Empress of Russia alongside a deliciously clownish Nicholas Hoult as her power-hungry and utterly twisted husband Emperor Peter III ... and earned her first Emmy nomination for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for her efforts.

Sadly, "The Great" ended in 2023 after only three seasons, although Fanning's next TV project, the crime drama miniseries "The Girl from Plainville," was well-received. In 2026, though, Fanning earned overwhelming acclaim and another Emmy nod for her lead role in "Margo's Got Money Troubles," a collaboration between A24 and Apple TV that proved to be one of the very best shows of the year. As a young single mother who launches an OnlyFans career as a colorful, coquettish alien to support her young son, Fanning is extraordinary as Margo, and it's clear that this ambitious and incredibly talented actor will keep racking up credits and accolades for years to come.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is currently in theaters.

#3556. Four Things You Can Do With Google Maps' New 'Ask Maps' Feature

Google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

Google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

To me, this is the most useful new feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is currently open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Plans can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google says this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

If you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

#3555. Christmas in July? Why Stop There?

Why do we let something like the calendar dictate our holidays? The fact that Thanksgiving and Christmas are just four weeks apart means by the time you’ve returned from November family visits, unpacked, shopped, decorated, done the party circuit, bought gifts, and maybe—maybe—worked for a few days, you have to turn around and celebrate again. It’s exhausting and expensive and too warp-speed to feel like that much of a good time. I’m not arguing to ban Christmas—which I am using as a catchall for nondenominational winter holidays, however that looks to you—what I am proposing is, in fact, much more exciting. I think we should switch the dates of Christmas and Valentine’s Day.

Consider it! Instead of condensing so much effort and so much merriment into such a ludicrously small window at the very end of the year with nothing but the bland hell of winter ahead of us, let’s maximize our time by stretching it out. Valentine’s Day is for romance, whether that means watching Bridget Jones’s Diary with friends, eating overpriced meals at candlelit restaurants, making cards, or mainlining chocolates. So on December 24, celebrate platonic love with friends—à la Galentine’s Day, except we should think of a better name—and maybe go on a date on the 25th. If that date goes well: bam! You now have a plus-one to a New Year’s Eve party and a midnight make out partner.

If the holiday season has wrapped by February 14, the weeks following are the shoulder season. Life is slow. But by the time everyone trickles back home from watching Die Hard in their pajamas or shopping post-Christmas sales or going to the gym, you only have to survive one month until the sweet relief of spring in late March. Nothing makes more sense for how to survive the long nights and cold of winter.

So we go all-in on spring. Mid-April is when it likely won’t snow again; around then you no longer need heat—at least in New York City—so let’s make that a national holiday celebrating warm weather with seasonal bouquets (tulips, lilacs, peonies), foraged ramps, and maybe specials on dry-cleaning winter coats or sales on shearling boots.

But why stop there? We in America could take a page from France, where May can have four(!) public holidays as a kind of summer practice run. I’d be more than happy to celebrate VE Day in solidarity: Liberté, égalité, holiday! In our version, maybe botanical gardens will be free to the public for picnics. Maybe amusement parks will be gratis? Maybe lobster rolls and strawberry shortcake will be handed out on the street? Can the first summer blockbuster of May be an annual event with free popcorn? This month of long weekends will culminate in Memorial Day barbecues, which is a perfect bookend to summer with Labor Day—no notes.

Let’s keep summer luxurious, so summer Fridays will not be at the discretion of employers but mandated by the government for those three months. The Fourth of July can stay where it is with the caveat that if it rains, we get to observe it on the next day forecast for hot dog weather. Nothing important happens in August—phone it in, federal holiday or not. Labor Day stays, of course. The week following it in New York is Fashion Week, which runs concurrently with the US Open for tennis—very busy but very social. We’re going to adopt that nationwide as a festive season soft launching the country into fall.

And finally, let’s turn our attention to that somber stretch of time between early September and Thanksgiving. We don’t get enough time off, so we will move Presidents’ Day from February to mid-October for another much-needed holiday. Then cook a big turkey dinner on Thanksgiving, see your extended family, watch football, whatever, and delight in the fact that you don’t have to do it again until February. But start figuring out your Valentine’s Day dates now—those prix fixe dinners with chocolate lava cakes really book up fast these days.

#3554. 5 Actors Who Should Play Q In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Movies

The next era of the "James Bond" movie franchise is upon us. After years of waiting and endless speculation, Robert Pattinson is officially the next Bond and is replacing Daniel Craig. The Craig era firmly and definitively came to an end in 2021 with "No Time to Die." Now? The former "Twilight" and current "The Batman" star gets to put his stamp on 007. But what about his supporting cast?

Making a new "Bond" film doesn't just mean casting a new MI6 agent. It means filling out some other key roles, and that includes Q, aka the quartermaster and head of Q Branch at MI6. This is historically the individual who outfits Bond with his various gadgets and field equipment for his missions. Ben Whishaw made his debut as Q in "Skyfall" during the Craig era, serving as one of only a small handful of actors to take on that responsibility.

The character made a brief appearance in "Dr. No" as "Major Boothroyd" played by Peter Burton, but for the lion's share of this franchise's existence, it was the late, great Desmond Llewelyn who played Q, with his tenure extending all the way from "From Russia with Love" to "The World is Not Enough." That was one heck of a run. Now, though, it's time for the next chapter.

So, who will suit up as Q for "Dune" director Denis Villeneuve and outfit Pattinson's Bond for his next mission? We're going to go over five actors who should be considered for the role, for various reasons. Let's get into it.

This may seem too obvious and perhaps even painful for the actor involved, but it also makes sense. Robert Pattinson's "James Bond" casting continued an unfortunate trend for Nicholas Hoult as he's always the bridesmaid, never the bride. He was the runner up for Batman in "The Batman" and the runner up for Superman in "Superman." Now? He was one of the finalists for Bond before Pattinson nabbed the role. It's been a rough run for the actor.

Be that as it may, much in the same way that missing out on Superman made him a damn fine Lex Luthor, he could be a very good Q in Denis Villeneuve's currently untitled "Bond" movie. For one, it's pretty darn easy to picture Hoult as a smart guy in a lab coat. His work as Beast in the "X-Men" films proved that well enough, and he's only become a better actor in the years since joining that franchise, so there's no question he could pull it off.

More importantly, Bond and Q have always had something of a playfully contentious relationship in the movies. "Pay attention, 007!" and all that jazz. Hoult might have a little bit of playful bitterness and/or jealousy to work with when it comes to Pattinson as Bond. That could provide a lot of on-screen fuel and chemistry for the dynamic between these two.

Now, would Hoult want to settle for Q after missing out on the big prize? That's unclear, but if he's open to it, this could be a fun option.

Samantha Morton is an actor who has been doing it at a very high level for a very long time, yet she remains somewhat unappreciated. Now, though, Morton has made herself more familiar to audiences as Circe in Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey," delivering a scene-stealing performance in a movie filled with A-listers who all brought their A game. That list of actors just so happens to include Robert Pattinson. So, even though the pair didn't share any screen time, their reunion here would be a nice story in and of itself.

But more than that, Morton is a wildly flexible performer of immense talent. From sci-fi movies like "Minority Report" to hit TV shows such as "The Walking Dead," she's been everywhere and done it all. Morton is often a pretty serious actor, too, and she could bring a stern quality to Q. At the same time, the role would allow her to loosen up a bit, which would undoubtedly be fun to see from an artist of her caliber.

Morton will also be in her 50s by the time filming on the next "James Bond" movie truly gets underway, so her age provides her with a believable wisdom that she could impart onto Pattinson's Bond. Indeed, there's something about the notion of a quartermaster in these movies that benefits from someone who feels like they lived a life before being relegated to Q Branch. It's been missing ever since Desmond Llewelyn passed, and Morton could bring it back with her own, unique twist.

If Denis Villeneuve and the brass at Amazon want to use the new Q for some dry comedic relief, as opposed to going the more serious route, it's hard to imagine a better fit for the role than Richard Ayoade. One of the most consistently funny British comedians of the current generation, it's almost too easy to picture him in a lab coat giving Robert Pattinson's 007 the business before he heads out on a mission.

Ayoade has a very distinct, very British, and at times delightfully dry sense of humor. It's the sort of trait that's easy to picture someone with Q's job having. Ayoade is also a damn fine writer and director, so he could be an asset to the production overall. Heck, NBC tried to remake "The IT Crowd" more than once and failed more than once, as Ayoade and the distinctive sense of humor he brought to that show are quite difficult to pull off.

This particular casting choice relies an awful lot on the direction of this new iteration of the franchise. Villeneuve is a pretty serious storyteller and, for that reason, Ayoade might be a long shot. That's not to say that he couldn't turn in a dramatic performance, but the benefit of casting him is foremost comedic relief. If Villeneuve strikes a balance between humor and grit, recalling something closer to "GoldenEye" than "Casino Royale," then it's easier to envision.

Basically, if the shoe fits, Ayoade feels like a slam dunk casting choice.

If the idea was just, "Let's find the very best actor we can and offer her the role of Q in this movie," then it would be tough to do better than Emma Thompson. These things are subjective, but she's a two-time Oscar winner and a five-time Oscar nominee who has been one of the best actors working pretty much for as long as we've known her name. If she says yes, you say thank you.

At first glance, it might make more sense to have Thompson play M rather than Q. And look, if Denis Villeneuve offered her the role of M, I'd happily get behind it. That said, some of Thompson's best work is on the more playful side, be it her turn in Hugh Jackman's must-watch murder mystery "The Sheep Detectives" or the criminally under-seen "Stranger Than Fiction." Yes, she's about as good as it gets when she puts on her serious hat in movies like "The Remains of the Day" as well. We can't forget that.

Q could give her an opportunity to have some fun while flexing every facet of her acting chops. A director like Villeneuve has a knack for getting the most out of great actors, even if it's in a smaller role. See: Dave Bautista in "Dune." As such, letting an actor as good as Thompson eat up the scenery in a "James Bond" movie as Q would be an asset to this new iteration of the franchise.

Would Thompson be interested in doing such a thing? Would she rather play a Bond villain? It's tough to say, but if this came up, and Thompsan entertained saying yes, that would pretty much be the end of the discussion. Finding a "better" actor is going to be tough.

Last, but certainly not least, we come to the most obvious of the bunch, if not the most realistic in this particular scenario. Ben Whishaw made his entry into the franchise during the Daniel Craig era. "Skyfall" remains the biggest "James Bond" movie ever, which just so happens to be the first time audiences saw Whishaw as Q. He remained on board for the rest of the Craig era, including "Spectre" and "No Time to Die." So, why not just have him stay on board for the Robert Pattinson era?

In most cases in modern franchise filmmaking, reboot means total reset. However, the "James Bond" movies aren't like any other property. Desmond Llewelyn was the quartermaster for every single Bond save for Craig. Judi Dench was the M for both Pierce Brosnan and Craig. You get the idea. This film series has always played it a little more fast and loose with continuity in that way. Granted, Amazon is now in the driver's seat, and it seems to be changing things up already. Specifically, Pattinson's Bond casting broke a 60-year-old 007 tradition, as he's the biggest established movie star to ever take on the part.

For that reason, it seems far more likely that Denis Villeneuve and Amazon will move forth with a total reboot. However, if they decide to keep some level of tradition alive, bringing Whishaw back wouldn't be a bad call. He's even a little older now, which might allow him to bring something a bit different to the role this time around. There's no denying that he had something unique to offer.

Again, this may not be the most realistic choice, but in many ways, it's the most logical one.

The new "James Bond" movie doesn't have a release date yet, so stay tuned.

#3553. 10 Shows Like 'Youth' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Sharon Horgan had a string of British hits (including a couple we'll talk about here), before scoring stated successes with Divorce, Shining Vale, and Bad Sisters. She's quickly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

This earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

When all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

Michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she says more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

She'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

It's been several years since the Daniel Craig era of James Bond concluded, and work on Bond 26 is currently underway. Of course, this past week there was some big news on the front, as it was finally confirmed that Robert Pattinson would play the new 007. All the while, many are still wondering who will be the next Bond Girl. My pick is Alexandra Daddario, and I'm not the only one who feels that way. Now, amid the rumors, Daddario is weighing in.

According to recent reports that have dropped, the race for the position of next Bond Girl is becoming quite interesting. So far, prediction market Kalshi’s got Margaret Qualley topping Sydney Sweeney for its pick, followed by names like Anya Taylor-Joy and Florence Pugh along with others. While Daddario’s not on that list, it's no surprise she's still been linked to Bond 26 speculation. While speaking to Hollywood ReelTime, the fan-favorite actress shared a level-headed take:

The internet says things. I don’t really know. (laughs) I mean, I’m very excited to see the Bond movie, but I don’t believe I’ll be in it. I don’t know. The internet can say anything, I guess.

Based on the Couples Weekend star's laughter throughout her response, I’m curious if she knows something we don’t. But, like her Hershey costar Finn Witrock said, “Never say never.” I personally think Daddario would do a great job, as she has more than enough charm to pull it off. When looking back at the most iconic Bond Girls throughout history, they've each had elements of seen glamour, intelligence, emotional depth and mystery, and Daddario can embody all of those attributes.

We clearly know the Mayfair Witches actress has the beauty that’ll surely make the MI6 agent swoon. Whether she's wowing us with an end-of-summer bikini or giving Hollywood glamour in a gorgeous backless dress, fashionista Daddario would be perfect for it. Not to mention, any Bond can fall under the spell of her piercing blue eyes.

Other than looking like a true beauty, though, the Texas Chainsaw 3D star has experience with action movies like the Percy Jackson films and San Andreas. Daddario has also played characters who are vulnerable and emotionally guarded. Through her award-recognized portrayal of Rachel in The White Lotus, she played a woman experiencing internal struggles and conflicting emotions about her husband.

Also, in True Detective, Daddario's character, Lisa, refuses to be disregarded while serving as a mistress to Detective Hart. So, with these two HBO roles alone, I believe Daddario can give both sensuality and substance while playing a Bond Girl. I also want to see her chemistry with Robert Pattinson. While the two have never done a project together, I can see them playing off each other well.

While we don’t know yet who will be the lucky lady to play the next Bond Girl, I'm keeping my fingers crossed for Alexandra Daddario to get the part. Hopefully, additional information on the upcoming film -- which is being directed by Denis Villeneuve -- will arrive sooner rather than later. In the meantime, though, you can watch Daddario in the 2026 movie release Hershey, which is in theaters now.

#3551. You Can Try WhatsApp's New Disappearing Text Messages Early

Like Snapchat messages, WhatsApp's "View Once" feature is a great way to send things you don't want living on your friends' devices. You can send voice messages, photos, and videos that will "self-destruct" after they're opened, limiting (if not eliminating) the risk of your friends keeping them forever. However, View Once has a major limitation: While WhatsApp will let you send voice memos and images that way, you can't use it to send texts, meaning every one you send will live on (unless you unsend it yourself).

That's now changing. As reported by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is now beta testing View Once for text messages, too. Soon enough, you'll be able to send voice memos, photos, videos, and texts as one-time-only messages. That way, you can send sensitive information via text—say, a password or an important account number—without worrying about it persisting. Here's how it works: You craft your text message as you usually do, but rather than tap the send button, you hold it. You'll see the usual "Schedule message" option, but once the feature rolls out, you'll also find a new "View Once" option as well.

As mentioned above, this feature is currently in testing, so it's only available to WhatsApp beta testers. What's more, only the Android version of the beta has access at the moment, so iOS beta testers are out of luck. (That said, the WhatsApp iOS beta is perpetually full, so there's not much you could do even if WhatsApp made this test available on iPhone.)

If you have an Android device, you can enroll in the WhatsApp beta to try out "View Once" text messages today. According to WABetaInfo, the feature is live as of WhatsApp version 2.26.45.6. To enroll, open the WhatsApp beta page on the Google Play store and enroll your account in the beta. If you don't have WhatsApp on your phone already, download it here; if you do, reload the page and install the latest update. This will update your existing WhatsApp app to the latest beta version.

#3550. Lesley Manville, Pierce Brosnan, and More Celebrate Violinist Joshua Bell at the Langham London

At the age of four, Joshua Bell was given his first violin, and he hasn’t put it down since. “I don’t remember falling in love with music,” says Bell. “Music has just been my life. I used to string rubber bands on my dresser drawers and make pitches by pulling the drawers out. I was fascinated with strings. It’s the closest instrument to the human voice. And I find it the most expressive instrument.”

Today, the Grammy Award–winning musician is one of the most celebrated classical violinists of his era. By 14, Bell was performing with the Philadelphia Orchestra, and would soon be touring the world. “I live in hotels 250 days a year,” says Bell of the nonstop schedule he has maintained since his teens. Specifically, Bell has been “staying at the Langham for decades now,” he says, referring to the regal central London hotel that first opened in 1865. “I chose it on my own because it was near one of my favorite halls in London, which is the Wigmore Hall. And now I stay with them whenever I’m traveling.”

That kinship was solidified over coupes of Champagne and hand-dived Orkney scallops, with the hotel celebrating Bell, a “Langham Luminary,” in its London ballroom packed with writers, artists, designers, and musicians.

Attendees included actor Simon Callow, House of Dragon actor Emily Carey, former British culture minister Ed Vaizey, Saturday Night Live UK cast producer Susie Hall, stage and television actor Indira Varma, and Verity actor Ismael Cruz Córdova.

Held in partnership with Vanity Fair, the evening marked the latest iteration of the Langham’s Luminaries in Residence program. The event series is continuation of the hotel’s legacy that brings together a diverse, influential community—an evocative reminder of prominent guests from its storied past, including Charles Dickens, Winston Churchill, George Orwell, Oscar Wilde, and Mark Twain.

“I’m not going to put my name in the same sentence as Toscanini or Mark Twain—who has stayed here, or Churchill, who has stayed here. But it’s cool to be part of the history,” says Bell. “So maybe someday, in a hundred years, there will be a violinist who might say that—that I stayed here. I don’t know, maybe that would mean something.”

It certainly does mean something. Pierce Brosnan and his wife, Keely Shaye Brosnan, “have been huge fans of Joshua for many, many years,” Brosnan tells me. “Keely went to go see him…I don’t know how many years back. Unfortunately, due to the LA traffic, she got there late, five minutes late, and they wouldn’t let her into the concert. So tonight is one of those nights.”

Bell, who performed mid-dinner with members of the Academy of St. Martin in the Fields—with a surprise appearance from his wife, soprano Larisa Martínez—brought about a collective catharsis.

Dazzling, fiery, and flamboyant, the experience of watching Bell up close is impossible to replicate. “I just think he’s incredibly soulful, and there’s something really elegant,” actor Russell Tovey tells me, before explaining how he actually discovered Bell via his Instagram algorithm.

For actor Lesley Manville, the event marked her introduction to Bell’s music. “I’m a bit embarrassed that he was not on my radar. But isn’t that nice to have a surprise like that?” says Manville. “Schubert’s String Quintet is one of my favorite pieces of music. It’s unbelievably beautiful. You think of a violin, you think of those strings. And it’s instant emotion. They just make you cry.”

There is a great power in being able to access the emotions of others, as Bell does.

“I think it is the ultimate gift to be able to make people happy,” says Brosnan. “My job is being an entertainer—to take the words of great writing and try to transform it into something that is meaningful and memorable.”

Speaking of entertaining, the week’s announcement that Robert Pattinson will be the next James Bond was front of mind. “I wish him every joy and every success. He and I made a movie a number of years ago called Remember Me. I played his father. So I was very, very pleased and joyful for his nomination and now his success, and I believe he will be magnificent.”

And that creative full circle is exactly what the night was advocating. “Our own Luminaries in Residence program reflects our belief that meaningful hospitality creates genuine connection with extraordinary talents with one another, and with arts,” Bob van den Oord, CEO of Langham Hospitality Group, explained as he took the stage. “The Langham isn’t simply a place to stay, but a place to gather, exchange ideas, and indeed celebrate.”

#3549. 10 Near-Perfect Netflix Sci-Fi Shows That Hook You in the First Scene

From mind-bending mysteries to dystopian futures, these Netflix sci-fi gems pull you in from minute one

Not every great sci-fi show starts with a bang, but the best ones grab your attention from the very first frame. Whether it’s an alien organism mutating a host in seconds, a gruesome public execution in the middle of a cultural revolution, or a child stepping into a smoke-filled battleground littered with corpses, the most compelling shows understand the power of a great first impression. These series offer something tangible enough to keep you glued to your seat before the opening credits even roll.

Spanning mind-bending mysteries, dystopian anthologies, sprawling futuristic epics, and some of the most ambitious animation on television, Netflix has delivered a fairly robust setlist of sci-fi shows over the years. With so many experiences to choose from (on Netflix and well beyond), finding that perfect sci-fi series that’s worth committing to can be quite the challenge, but the most thrilling among them make that decision easy with unforgettable premises and scientific mysteries that demand to be solved.

Opening doors to strange new worlds, fractured realities, and futures both wondrous and terrifying, these 10 near-perfect Netflix sci-fi series will pull you into the unknown from the get. Ranked from exceptional genre standouts to bona fide masterpieces, each leaves a mark that lingers long after the first scene fades to black.

From the same minds behind Dark, Jantje Friese and Baran bo Odar’s 1899 drops you aboard the Kerberos, a steamliner carrying a multinational group of passengers from England to New York. Though a seemingly rudimentary voyage at sea, it’s quickly thrown off course when a cryptic signal lures the crew toward the Prometheus, the Kerberos’ sister ship that vanished four months prior. What begins as a routine transatlantic crossing no sooner turns into a psychological nightmare, where the vast isolation of the open ocean only fuels the growing claustrophobia on board.

Few sci-fi mysteries establish such an oppressive atmosphere so quickly. The pilot surrounds its passengers with endless stretches of dark ocean, cramped corridors, and strange occurrences that suggest the ship is hiding secrets beyond anyone's understanding. Every conversation feels loaded with unspoken history, while the discovery of the abandoned Prometheus introduces a chilling mystery that only grows more sinister from there. In its infinite wisdom, Netflix canceled 1899 after just one season, leaving the story’s larger puzzle unresolved, but its premiere remains a remarkably effective exercise in mounting dread, and is perfect for fans of movies like Ghost Ship and Triangle.

Adapted from Liu Cixin's acclaimed science-fiction trilogy, 3 Body Problem traces humanity's encounter with an alien civilization across multiple decades. Its story begins amid the political violence of China’s Cultural Revolution, where a disillusioned young astrophysicist makes a decision that alters the course of history, before jumping to a present-day group of Oxford scientists grappling with seemingly impossible phenomena. What initially appears to be a series of isolated crises rapidly escalates as a countdown appears in people's vision, particle accelerators return nonsensical results, the night sky blinks in code, and hyper-advanced alien tech reveals that an incoming hostile invasion fleet is already systematically crippling human scientific progress.

The opening sequence wastes little time establishing the horrors that will shape everything that follows. During a struggle in 1960s Beijing, physicist Ye Zhetai is publicly denounced and beaten to death for his scientific beliefs. It's a brutal introduction to the ideological persecution of the era, but its consequences reach far beyond the immediate tragedy. By connecting this historical trauma to the scientific mysteries unfolding decades later, the 3 Body Problem establishes a compelling link between humanity's capacity for cruelty and the possibility of a threat that could change the fate of the entire species.

Love, Death & Robots is a rather unique series to include on this list given that it isn't one cohesive story but a group of smaller, bite-sized narratives. Bringing together diverse international animation studios, it explores various sci-fi themes, like cybernetics, artificial intelligence, hyper-violence, and surreal cosmic horrors across wildly different visual styles. Conceived by Tim Miller and David Fincher, the series serves as a spiritual successor to classic speculative sci-fi and heavy metal comics, and offers four seasons of compelling sci-fi.

Although Love, Death & Robots is an anthology that allows you to jump around between episodes, its first installment, “Three Robots,” makes a compelling case for starting from the beginning. As you’d expect from the title, the episode follows three robots as they explore the ruins of a human civilization, balancing dark comedy with a surprisingly bleak vision of humanity's future. It's a fitting introduction to an anthology that rarely lets its sci-fi spectacle exist without an unsettling idea lurking beneath the surface. I'd be remiss if I didn't also mention my personal favorite, “Beyond the Aquila Rift,” an episode best watched totally fresh.

Black Mirror examines the darker implications of technological progress, exposing the ways our advancements can amplify humanity's cruelties, insecurities, and appetite for spectacle. Much like Love, Death, & Robots, its anthology format allows you to approach the series on your own terms, moving between near-future dystopias, digital nightmares, and biting social satire, with each story offering a terrifying but very different vision of what happens when innovation outpaces our moral judgment, resulting in a modern successor to The Twilight Zone.

Charlie Brooker’s seminal anthology series has evolved significantly over its run, but its core potency remains remarkably intact. Early masterclasses like "The Entire History of You" and "White Bear" set a gold standard by weaponizing technological near-futures to interrogate human cruelty and obsession. Recent highlights like "Loch Henry" and "Beyond the Sea" prove the show hasn't lost its edge. Whether dissecting the true-crime genre's voyeuristic exploitation or sending mechanical synth-replicas into alternate-1960s space, Black Mirror demonstrates that its central thesis was never just about screen addiction, but about the dark impulses of the people holding the device.

Based on the manga by Naoki Urasawa and Takashi Nagasaki (itself a reimagining of Osamu Tezuka's Astro Boy), Pluto transforms a classic robot adventure into a contemplative science-fiction murder mystery unlike any other. In a future where humans and sophisticated robots coexist, Europol inspector Gesicht investigates a string of killings targeting both people and machines. The victims are connected to a history of conflict and political upheaval, suggesting that the crimes are part of something much larger than an isolated series of murders.

The first episode opens with the destruction of Mont Blanc, a beloved Swiss robot known for his peaceful nature, before introducing Gesicht and his investigation. The discovery of strange, hornlike debris near the scene gives the murder an almost ritualistic, True Detective quality. Yet Pluto is less interested in shock for its own sake than in the questions raised by the violence: Can a machine experience grief? What does it mean to possess a conscience? And can a society that claims to have moved beyond prejudice truly escape the hatred that shaped its past? Those questions lend the premiere a melancholic weight that lingers well beyond its central crime.

The Duffer Brothers' Stranger Things draws on the suburban adventures, supernatural horror, and coming-of-age stories that defined much of 1980s popular culture, akin to the likes of It, Stand by Me, and The Goonies. Set in Hawkins, Indiana, the series begins with the disappearance of Will Byers, a young boy whose friends and family soon discover that something deeply unnatural is happening in their seemingly unremarkable town. The arrival of Eleven, a mysterious girl with psychokinetic abilities, further entangles their lives with a secretive government research facility and a terrifying alternate dimension.

The premiere's opening scene belongs to an unfortunate scientist racing through the corridors of Hawkins National Laboratory. Alarms blare, lights flicker, and an unseen creature closes in as he scrambles toward an elevator. Just when it seems he might escape, something drags him upward into the darkness. The sequence lasts only a short moment, but it’s enough to nail down the show's ability to make the familiar feel frighteningly unsafe. By the time the story shifts to a group of kids playing Dungeons & Dragons, the threat looming over Hawkins has already hooked you like Vecna’s curse itself.

Cyberpunk: Edgerunners takes place in the same dystopian universe as Cyberpunk 2077, bringing Night City's excesses to life through explosive animation and a deeply tragic coming-of-age story. The first season follows David Martinez, a teenager from a working-class background whose attempts to survive the city's punishing social order eventually lead him into the world of cybernetically enhanced mercenaries known as edgerunners. In Night City, almost anything can be bought, upgraded, or weaponized, but the human cost of that progress is impossible to escape.

Rather than introducing David immediately, the premiere begins with a small glimpse of what the world of Night City can do to a person. A heavily augmented soldier tears through a squad of armed officers in a frenzy of overwhelming violence, offering a terrifying demonstration of cyberware pushed beyond its limits. The sequence is later revealed through a braindance recording, a form of immersive digital playback that lets viewers experience recorded events. Such framing is crucial to understanding the world of Night City, where even the brutality of a cyberpsycho's rampage becomes not just entertainment but a commodity. With Cyberpunk: Edgerunners season 2 another standout hit, there’s no better time to dive into its mean streets.

The OA resists easy categorization, weaving together science fiction with psychological drama to answer questions about the nature of consciousness. At its center is Prairie Johnson, a blind young woman who disappeared for seven years before unexpectedly returning to her adoptive parents with the ability to somehow see. Insisting she be called the “OA,” Prairie refuses any explanation as to where she has been, or how she recovered her sight, a series of oddities that swiftly form the foundation for a mystery that expands beyond the boundaries of ordinary reality.

The series kicks off with shaky cellphone footage of Prairie running across a bridge before jumping into the water below. The sequence is brief, disorienting, and deliberately short on context, leaving viewers down that rabbit hole of wonder, questioning what could have driven Prairie to such an extreme act, and what it might mean in the context of the story writ large. Her subsequent return, sight restored and past shrouded in uncertainty, only deepens those mysteries further. Few premieres make the act of asking questions feel so essential to the experience, and The OA turns that uncertainty into its defining strength.

Developed by Riot Games and animated by French studio Fortiche, Arcane is inarguably one of the best shows on Netflix. The series, in all intents and purposes, expands the world of League of Legends, but does it through an emotionally rich story about class conflict, political ambition, and fractured family bonds. Its central tension lies between Piltover, a prosperous city embracing technological advancement, and Zaun, the neglected undercity struggling beneath its wealth and influence. Shaped by the violence and inequality that separate the two communities, sisters Vi and Powder end up on opposite sides of a brewing war as Hextech magic and the street-drug Shimmer threaten to destroy both cities.

The premiere opens with a haunting image of the sisters walking across a bridge strewn with bodies in the aftermath of a violent uprising. Smoke hangs in the air as a mournful melody accompanies their passage through the devastation, while the young girls struggle to comprehend the world that has been left to them. The sequence communicates the human cost of the conflict before the series even begins exploring its political and personal consequences. Fortiche's painterly animation also gives the scene a storybook beauty, made all the more affecting by the brutality it depicts.

Like all great mysteries, Dark begins with a familiar small-town tragedy. But as a missing child case unravels into a web of temporal paradoxes, Winden gradually transforms into one of television's most intricate science fiction puzzles. The sudden disappearances expose generations of buried secrets and tangled family histories, forcing characters to confront anomalies that shatter their understanding of cause and effect. While its dense mythology can be demanding, the series grounds its mind-bending scope in deeply human fears, like losing loved ones, repeating past mistakes, and realizing that those closest to us can sometimes be total strangers.

The pilot sets that tone before the central mystery even begins. A voiceover meditates on the nature of time as the camera moves through a dimly lit room, where a man named Michael Kahnwald has died by suicide. The unsettling imagery and somber narration immediately establish a world weighed down by the inescapable pull of the past. Dark slowly plants clues that will eventually connect Winden's missing children to a much larger mystery, one that is as mind-boggling as it is emotionally gripping. Its opening is less a conventional hook than an invitation to enter a world where every answer seems to create another burning question.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3548. Why Sylvester Stallone's Father In I Play Rocky Looks So Familiar

Peter Farrelly's biopic "I Play Rocky" tells the story of a young Sylvester Stallone (Anthony Ippolito) as he rises through his early, sketchy acting career, eventually coming to write and star in 1976's "Rocky," itself one of the best sports movies ever made. The film doesn't sugarcoat Stallone's early struggles, including his run-down apartment, his inability to land good roles as a young actor going by the name of Mike (leading him to work on an adult feature), and the fact that, at one point, he had to sleep on the street.

It also depicts the verbal abuse that he suffered at the hands of his domineering father, Frank Sr, who runs a barbershop and is hardly encouraging. When Stallone relates his acting dreams, Frank tells his son that he isn't handsome enough to be a movie star. Ouch, dad.

Frank is played by Matt Dillon, who exploded onto the cinematic scene in 1979 thanks to his role in Jonathan Kaplan's "Over the Edge," a film so beloved that it inspired both Richard Linklater and Kurt Cobain. Dillon rose to prominence shortly after that, appearing in movies like "Little Darlings," "Liar's Moon," and Francis Ford Coppola's S.E. Hinton adaptations "The Outsiders" and "Rumble Fish."

Indeed, for a spell during the 1980s, Dillon was a teen heartthrob, and his intense performance style and tenacity dictated a steady stream of high-profile work as he got older. That includes his role in Gun Van Sant's 1989 picture "Drugstore Cowboy" (which caused quite a stir) and his turn in Cameron Crowe's 1992 movie "Singles" (one of the 1990s' defining films). From there, he collaborated with Van Sant again when he played a pushy husband in 1995's "To Die For" and had a key role in Frank Oz's mainstream 1997 queer comedy "In & Out.

Listing all of Matt Dillon's credits here would take up too much space. Just know that he has been a creative force in Hollywood for, gosh, almost 50 years, and has constantly teamed up with prominent directors, among them Garry Marshall, Arthur Penn, Allison Anders, Lars Von Trier, and Wes Anderson. His role as  Frank Stallone Sr. in "I Play Rocky" isn't even the first time Dillon has played a real person. In fact, he previously played Marlon Brando in the Maria Schneider biopic "Being Maria" and Henri Chinaski, Charles Bukowski's literary alter ego, in the 2005 film "Factotum."

"I Play Rocky" itself marks the second time Dillon has worked with Peter Farrelly, as he also appeared in the Farrelly Bros.' 1998 ultra-hit comedy "There's Something About Mary," playing the toothsome character of Pat. That same year, he played a sleazy, double-crossing teacher in the thriller "Wild Things" and thereafter worked on everything from Disney films ("Herbie: Fully Loaded") to the notorious Best Picture Oscar-winning "Crash," whose own director, Paul Haggis, later admitted didn't deserve to be crowned Best Picture. Nevertheless, Dillon is excellent in it.

Even now, Dillon shows no signs of slowing down. And while he specializes in playing tough guys and aggressive heavies, he's quite capable of other things, with "Drugstore Cowboy" displaying his range with what, for my money, is his best performance. But then, there are so many to choose from. He does a good job as an oppressive father figure in the syrupy but highly watchable "I Play Rocky," too, embodying a hard-working barber who may love his son but doesn't think much of him. It's a solid, dark turn for a longtime, hardworking actor.

Grand Theft Auto VI came out on November 19, and literally one day after that, it was announced that it had hit $3.79 billion in sales. That’s a seriously impressive number. I mean, it took Taylor Swift nearly two years to make $2 billion with her highly profitable Eras Tour. GTA did more than that in one day. However, while that is quite mind-blowing to think about, fans aren’t so impressed by this comparison.

To get into the specifics, it was reported by Rockstar Games that GTA VI has reached $3.79 billion in sales as of November 20, per The AP. It also stated that 32.5 million units were sold in pre-release. When People published a story on what the video game had reportedly made, it prominently noted that it had already outgrossed Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour.

Looking at the Eras Tour, specifically, after its 21-month run, it racked up $2 billion in tickets sold and over 10 million people attended the concerts (its proshot was also a major box office success and can now be streamed with a Disney+ subscription). The NYT, that’s “double the gross ticket sales of any other concert tour in history.” Also, reportedly, the tour’s average gross per night was between $14 and $17 million.

Considering the fact that both the Eras Tour and GTA VI were highly anticipated events – Taylor Swift hadn’t toured in six years before Eras, and fans waited 13 years for the new GTA – I get why this comparison is staggering. It’s honestly wild that it took GTA one day to do more than what Taylor Swift did in a little less than two years.

However, many fans made it clear they weren’t that impressed by this comparison.

When you really think about it, comparing GTA to the Eras Tour is like comparing apples and oranges. One is a concert tour; the other is a video game. Yes, they’re both major moments of monoculture. However, that’s kind of all they have in common. So, that left people commenting things like this on People’s post about the video game outgrossing Swift’s tour:

Something many comments pointed out was that there was a cap on how many people could attend the Eras Tour. There are only so many people you can fit in a stadium. Anyone can buy and play Grand Theft Auto VI. So, it makes sense that it could make more than the tour in such a short period of time.

It might be more fitting to compare GTA VI's release to this year’s box office, considering almost anyone can go to the movies if they want to. In one day, this video game managed to make more than the current highest-grossing film on the 2026 movie schedule, which is Spider-Man: Brand New Day (the film made more than $2 billion worldwide during its run in theaters this summer).

Then, if we really want to compare apples to apples, Grand Theft Auto V generated $1 billion in sales during its first three days. In total, the 2013 game accounts for over 230 million of the franchise's 470 million units sold. It would seem the sixth installment is well on its way to beating its predecessor.

Anyway, getting back to GTA and The Eras Tour, overall, I agree with fans in a way, because this is a hard comparison to make. However, it’s also undeniable that the release of GTA VI and The Eras Tour are two of the biggest pop culture moments in recent history, and it is kind of wild that the video game managed to outgross the concert series in one day.
