#3518. Clint Eastwood's Unforgiven Was Almost A Francis Ford Coppola Movie

The very best Western that the legendary Clint Eastwood ever made was a very nearly directed by Francis Ford Coppola. Clint Eastwood's relationship with the Western stretches back to the beginning of his career, when he became an international star playing Rowdy Yates in the television series Rawhide. His casting in Sergio Leone's Dollars Trilogy subsequently established him as one of the genre's defining presences, helping to popularize the Spaghetti Western around the world.

Eastwood eventually took that experience behind the camera, making his directorial debut with Play Misty for Me (1971) before turning to the Western with High Plains Drifter (1973). Over the following decades, he developed a distinctive approach to the genre, directing and starring in films that questioned the morality of traditional gunslingers.

Eastwood’s Westerns became increasingly interested in the consequences of violence and the mythology surrounding the American frontier. That evolution culminated in Unforgiven (1992), widely regarded as Eastwood's greatest Western and a film that almost ended up in the hands of The Godfather’s Francis Ford Coppola.

Unforgiven is a critically acclaimed post-western with Eastwood in the starring role as well as directing. Screenwriter David Webb Peoples wrote the original screenplay in 1976, giving it the rather less marketable title The Cut-Whore Killings. The story concerned an aging outlaw drawn back into violence, but its brutal subject matter and unromantic view of the Old West were hardly a conventional pitch for a genre that Hollywood had largely put aside.

Francis Ford Coppola acquired the rights in the early 1980s. Fresh from the success of The Godfather and Apocalypse Now, the director had the stature to make an ambitious Western a serious prospect. However, Coppola couldn't secure the financing to get Peoples' screenplay into production.

Coppola’s option eventually expired, leaving the project available to another filmmaker. Eastwood subsequently optioned the screenplay, although it would still take several years to reach the screen.

Eastwood had actually encountered the script while looking for a writer to work with in the early 1980s. In an August 1992 interview with the Los Angeles Times, he recalled being impressed by it, only to discover that Coppola still held the rights. When Eastwood's team contacted Peoples' agent, the timing was remarkably fortunate. Coppola had surrendered the option just two days earlier, so Eastwood bought the screenplay and kept it.

Although Eastwood had secured the rights, he didn't immediately rush into production. He was busy making other films, including Pale Rider (1985), and recognized that the central character required an older performer. William Munny is a retired outlaw who has attempted to leave his murderous past behind, raising his children on a struggling farm after the death of his wife.

When a young bounty hunter offers him the chance to earn money by killing two cowboys, Munny reluctantly returns to the life he has tried to escape. Eastwood understood that the role would mean more if he waited. Speaking to the Los Angeles Times in August 1992, he explained: "I always thought it was a little gem, but I figured I had to age into it."

It was an unusually candid admission from a star whose screen identity had been built around playing formidable men. Rather than repeat the hard-edged gunslinger persona that had made him famous, Eastwood wanted to portray a man whose physical decline and painful memories made violence far less glamorous.

Eastwood finally brought the project to the screen in 1991, starring alongside Morgan Freeman, Gene Hackman and Richard Harris. The resulting film is a revisionist Western in the most meaningful sense. Its violence is ugly, frightening and consequential, rather than an opportunity for the hero to show off his shooting skills. It refuses to offer a comfortable division between heroic gunslingers and villainous outlaws, interrogating the myths that Eastwood's own earlier Westerns had popularized.

Unforgiven was acclaimed by critics and became a major awards success. It won four Oscars, including Best Picture and Best Director for Eastwood, as well as Best Supporting Actor for Hackman and Best Film Editing for Joel Cox. Peoples was nominated for Best Original Screenplay, while Eastwood received a Best Actor nomination. Unforgiven also marked a significant moment in Eastwood's career as a filmmaker, earning recognition for a mature, carefully controlled work that challenged the conventions of the genre he had helped define.

#3517. Apple TV’s New 8-Part Crime Thriller Is Already a No. 1 Streaming Hit

The elaborate bank robbery story is finding a big streaming audience

Anthony Mackie has spent decades building an impressive Hollywood career, moving between blockbuster franchises, action movies, and acclaimed television projects. Now, the actor is adding another streaming success to his filmography. His latest project, a new thriller that takes a high-stakes premise and puts Mackie front and center, has wasted little time attracting attention on Apple TV.

The eight-episode series 12 12 12 premiered on Apple TV on Nov. 13, and it took just three days to reach No. 1 on the platform's worldwide streaming chart, according to FlixPatrol. The crime thriller has quickly established itself as one of the service's most-watched new releases, beating out several established Apple TV favorites in the process.

12 12 12 follows a disgraced FBI agent named Jack Strickland (Mackie) and an American career criminal named Paul Galvin (Jamie Dornan), who become entangled in a dangerous game of cat and mouse across Europe.

At the center of the story is an ambitious attempt to rob a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich. However, the series takes an unusual approach to telling its heist story, with each episode unfolding across three different timelines: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the robbery itself, and the 12 days that follow.

Despite its strong streaming debut, 12 12 12 has received a mixed response from critics and audiences so far. The series currently holds a 67% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes, alongside a 47% audience score. Critics have praised the chemistry between Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan, as well as the show's ambitious three-timeline storytelling, but some have criticized its convoluted structure and familiar heist-thriller tropes.

#3515. ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.]

At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

For her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

When Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

#3513. Josh Hutcherson Addresses Peeta Mellark's Legacy & Teases Future Hunger Games Return

An avid comic book fan since she first read "Stan Lee's Soapbox," Allison Hambrick is your friendly neighborhood generalist writer. Journalism, editing, media production, copywriting—she does it all. From her very first blog post about Smallville as a primary schooler, Allison developed a passion for superheroes and the entertainment industry at large.

This article contains mild spoilers for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on The Reaping.

Josh Hutcherson is reflecting on his time with The Hunger Games as its latest entry, Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters.

Hutcherson has been a part of the film franchise since its 2012 debut, playing the lovable baker boy Peeta Mellark. Alongside Jennifer Lawrence's Katniss Everdeen, Peeta is "reaped" from District 12 to participate in the 74th Hunger Games, a fight to the death for the morally corrupt Capitol's enjoyment and as a reminder that the Districts are under their thumb. The two form an unlikely but strong bond that later becomes instrumental as Katniss ultimately leads the fight against the Capitol.

The Young Adult dystopian franchise, based on Suzanne Collin's hit novels, has spawned six films, the first four of which chronicled Katniss' story. The latter two movies have been prequels. The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes followed the original series' villain, Coriolanus Snow, in his youth, while The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping recounted the tragic backstory of Katniss and Peeta's mentor, Haymitch Abernathy.

Longterm fans of The Hunger Games received a treat when the epilogue of Sunrise on the Reaping featured cameos by Lawrence, Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson. Recently, Hutcherson discussed having the opportunity to reunite with his costars on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, stating: "what's cool about this group is no matter how much time and distance passes when we get back together, it's just... the dynamics fall back into it."

Hutcherson also addressed the legacy of The Hunger Games and how it felt to come back after a decade for his Sunrise on the Reaping cameo."It's a weird mix of like having a nostalgic feeling and being so proud of the world that we got to help build," the Bridge to Terabithia star explained. "And it's like handing off the torch to the next generation [which] feels very cool." However, he then added: "it also makes me kind of like, 'damn, I wanted to be in it more.'"

While Hutcherson initially struggled with the global stardom that came with The Hunger Games, he has an affection for the franchise and the role of Peeta, one that makes him game for a comeback. Discussing the ending of the series, the actor stated:

I didn't want to say goodbye to the character. I didn't want to say goodbye to the world. I definitely didn't want to say goodbye to the people that we were making them [with]. But it was such an all-encompassing, life-changing type of recognition that, you know, I to this day don't like.

According to Hutcherson, he didn't know when or if he would get the call to return, but when he did, he "threw [his] cane like [Grandpa Joe} and was just like bebopping around" from excitement. "I had heard no rumblings of it," Hutcherson continued. "And it was something that I'd always wondered and hoped if there would be some version of... But like I said back then and I say now, it comes from whatever Suzanne wherever she takes the story. I'm happy that it came back to us in a way."

As for whether he would return, Hutcherson only offered one condition: "if there was a way that it made sense and Suzanne wrote something, I would absolutely do it."

#3510. Eight Important Router Settings You Should Check (or Change)

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Your router is a key piece of your home network, as it connects all of your other devices to the internet. This also makes it a highly valuable target for attackers and can leave your data vulnerable—especially if you simply plug your router in with its default settings unchanged. Whether your router is brand new or it's been a while since you audited your existing setup, these are the key settings to check and change right now.

Your router's security protocol determines how encryption and authentication work to protect data that's transmitted over your network. WPA3 Personal is the newest standard and the most secure, so if it's available on your router, enable it. It's compatible with devices that support Wi-Fi 6. Some older devices may not work with WPA3, in which case the WPA2/WPA3 Transitional mixed mode is a good alternative. At minimum, set your router to WPA2 Personal (AES).

Some routers ship with factory default login credentials, which are the username and password you need to access your device's admin dashboard. (This is not the same as your network name or wifi password, which you set up later.) Default router passwords are searchable online, which leaves your router's admin settings open to anyone. Once you get into your dashboard for the first time, change the default credentials and enable two-factor authentication for your admin account if available.

While some newer routers do have unique, device-specific defaults, it's a good idea to check this setting and ensure it's secure. If you're prompted to create custom admin credentials during the setup process, do it.

Your network name, or SSID, is how your network appears when you search for available wifi. By default, this may be the name of the router brand or a short string of characters, but you should choose something unique to your network. Make sure there's no identifying personal information, such as your name or house number. While you may be tempted to hide your network and obscure your SSID, this may actually make your information less secure, so keep this setting disabled. You can, however, add "_nomap" to the end of your network name, which prevents your router's physical coordinates from being mapped by location databases.

The password to access your network should also be unique and secure and should not include obvious personal information. One option to keep it memorable and easy to type is to create a passphrase using five to seven unrelated words that, combined, have at least 16 characters.

Being able to log into your router's admin dashboard from anywhere may be useful if you have complex networking needs or troubleshooting issues that often have to be addressed when you're away from home, but it also leaves an entry point open for attackers. Turn off remote management to prevent anyone from accessing your dashboard unless they are on your network. (This is also a great reason to have strong, unique admin credentials.)

Two additional settings that leave your network vulnerable are Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) and Universal Plug and Play (UPnP). The former lets users connect to your network with a PIN, which can be vulnerable to brute-force attacks. The latter allows smart devices to easily connect to your network—but this also allows malware to spread more readily. You may need to have UPnP on in order to connect devices initially but should disable it afterward.

Any easy win for your network security is segmenting traffic to different networks, so if one is compromised, the data on the others remain unaffected. Many wifi routers have a "guest mode," which creates a separate SSID and password that you can share with visitors instead of giving them your primary network credentials. You can also set up a separate network for all of your smart home and IoT devices so exploitable vulnerabilities in these devices don't put your computers, phones, and other connected devices at risk too.

Routers run a type of software—called firmware—just like any other device. Firmware controls the router's core functions and is not immune to vulnerabilities, which can be exploited by bad actors. And, just like other types of software, manufacturers occasionally push updates to patch these flaws. Check your router's dashboard to see if automatic updates are toggled on. Some devices require an opt-in for auto updates during setup, so you should enable them if they are off. Some routers may even require manual updates—in this case, set a monthly or quarterly (at minimum) calendar reminder to check for patches.

#3509. Former Blade Director Reveals What Went Wrong With The Ill-Fated Marvel Movie

"It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script"

Director Bassam Tariq, who was previously attached to direct the Mahershala Ali Blade movie that never came to fruition, was candid that the lack of a strong, complete script caused the Marvel Cinematic Universe movie to fall apart before it even started shooting.

The production timeline of the MCU Blade movie was brutal. It was first announced at San Diego Comic-Con in 2019 and was supposed to come out in 2023. Tariq signed on as director in 2021, and pre-production seemed in full swing by the summer of 2022, but Tariq stepped away from directing that September. While director Yenn Demange was then attached to the project, the 2023 actor's strike and ongoing production problems pushed the movie back even further.

Demange left the project in June 2024, and by 2025, the film had completely fizzled out. Ali has shared that he has moved on from wanting to play Blade, and he and Tariq subsequently collaborated on the action movie Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother. Speaking to The New Arab about the movie, Tariq was pretty transparent about why he walked away from making it.

"It was funny and strange to start casting and building without a proper script. You're sitting there and explaining to actors what their role will be, and they just have to believe you," he explained. "That's also very dangerous because if the text comes and it doesn't add up to what you were saying, your credibility gets completely shot. All I have is my integrity, and I've been thinking about that a lot. If you're the bearer of bad news to your actors, but you're not the one making any of these decisions — and it's actually coming from a corporate entity — that's not a great way to be a director."

Ultimately, Tariq's big takeaways from his work on Blade were that "life's too short to make shit films" and that he wants full control over the scripts for the movies he makes going forward. That was the case for Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which has received rave reviews.

It's well documented that Marvel movies don't often start production with locked scripts, and major changes to the story and certain action set pieces can happen mid-production. In Blade's case, that process didn't seem to work particularly well for Tariq as a director, and the movie fell apart as a result. While it's definitely a bummer that we'll never see Tariq and Ali's take on a Blade movie, we at least got Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother out of it.

#3507. ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 New York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.]

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.)

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the New York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

#3505. What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole new task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro said. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and said, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”

With no endgame to her harassment in sight, Marcia's next move is up in the air.

At first glance, Marcia seems like nothing more than a difficult boss. She’s somewhat manipulative. She's incredibly nice to everyone until she suddenly becomes overly critical, berating the 911 operators for being too emotional on calls and threatening to let AI take over their jobs. Then, she targets Cammie by playing the 911 call of her husband’s death in front of everyone. As harsh as that is, it's still "bad boss" territory. However, the revelation that she’s the one prank-calling Cammie turns it into a personal vendetta.

In the second episode she appeared in, Marcia told Cammie that she lost her son to a drunk driver when he was about 12 years old. Between that, the emphasis on not tying up the call center lines, and the harassment of Cammie, it makes one wonder if Cammie was the operator who answered the call about Marcia’s son, but got to it too late to help because the changes she was making weren't fully implemented, and the call was forced to hold. That would make Marcia’s efforts to tear Cammie down make sense, at least.

However, Marcia’s son had to have died at least a couple of years ago, so if she’s been plotting to find a way to become head of the call center solely to make crank calls, that’s wild (and honestly, not a great revenge plot). That leaves the question of where Marcia is headed with all of this, and how far 9-1-1: Nashville season 2 is willing to let her go. If crank calls are just the start, numerous possibilities could follow, from swatting to murder (depending on how dark the show wants to go this season).

The impact of Marcia’s villainy on Cammie, her family, her boyfriend, and the rest of the firefighting family depends on how her harassment evolves next. If she keeps up the crank calls, it will definitely affect Cammie’s mental health; that might even be the point, since, as Cammie’s boss, Marcia keeps saying she's responsible for the employees' mental health and well-being. Cammie’s mental health suffering gives Marcia the perfect opportunity to fire her from the call center, which might be all she’s aiming for.

ABC has confirmed its 2027 midseason premiere dates, confirming when viewers can expect new episodes of Will Trent, Shifting Gears, and many more.

It’s doubtful, though, that Cammie wouldn’t be back at her job in a few weeks (she’s the steadiest character on the show and 9-1-1: Nashville needs her), but it would create fantastic drama for a few episodes. Of course, if Marcia decides to take things further by putting Cammie actively in harm’s way, the consequences for everyone could be devastating. Doing that would put Marcia in harm’s way, too, though, because it’s safe to say the entire 113 (and Blythe) would come down in full force to protect Cammie.

That decision would likely end with Marcia behind bars. If 9-1-1: Nashville wants to keep her around long-term, though, she would need to actually have an honest conversation with Cammie. There would be no one better than Cammie to understand what it's like to have a loved one die because 911 didn't immediately answer a call. While that seems like the most reasonable option, Marcia has proven to be entirely unreasonable, so where her actions lead in the future remains to be seen.

9-1-1: Nashville returns Thursday, January 7, 2027, at 9 PM ET on ABC.

#3502. Clint Eastwood's Greatest War Epic Still Hits Hard After 20 Years

Clint Eastwood is a legend, of course. You can just look at all the movies he starred in over many decades to get a sense of just how legendary he was, all before taking into account how many classics he happened to direct (the movies in the Dollars trilogy, Dirty Harry, and Where Eagles Dare are all among the classics that only star Eastwood without him officially doing work behind the camera, too). But you should totally take into account the movies he directed. Honestly, some of the best movies he starred in also happened to be ones he directed. Just look at Unforgiven, Million Dollar Baby, and Gran Torino, for starters.

There are also movies Eastwood directed that he didn’t star in. Perhaps Mystic River is the most well-known of those, but not long after that movie, he also directed a pair of World War II movies that were hugely impressive, and he was solely behind the camera for those. For reasons that'll be explained near the end of this whole article, both are essential, but Flags of Our Fathers is arguably more of an epic out of the two, and the one that is perhaps best watched first. Also, it was released a couple of months before its companion film, Letters from Iwo Jima, so that does also make it potentially better to tackle first.

With these two movies, they're concerned with the Battle of Iwo Jima, essentially, depicting it from two different perspectives. To stick with Flags of Our Fathers for now, to outline what it’s about, it’s the American perspective of the battle, essentially. It’s a real-life battle fought as part of World War II, so if you think it’s a spoiler to say the Americans win, get outta here. Stop being ridiculous. But also, if you don’t know anything about this particular event during World War II, for whatever reason, the fact that the Americans won over the Japanese is clear early on. The focus here isn't as much about the lead-up to the battle or the battle itself; not in the way that Letters from Iwo Jima kind of is.

There are visceral combat scenes, sure, but most of the drama in Flags of Our Fathers takes place after the fighting’s over.

Flags of Our Fathers does some interesting things structurally, since so much of the movie is about the aftermath of the battle, and the way trauma lingers for those who survived it. There are visceral combat scenes, sure, but most of the drama in Flags of Our Fathers takes place after the fighting’s over. The act of raising the flag on Iwo Jima, alluded to in the film’s title, is ultimately what so much of the movie is about. There’s an element of propaganda to that event and the famous photo, and Flags of Our Fathers is largely an interesting and thought-provoking exploration of how that photo came to be taken, and what it meant for some of the people ultimately involved in its capturing/construction.

The runtime of Flags of Our Fathers doesn’t necessarily suggest you're in for an epic, but still, something being more than two hours long is fairly lengthy. And maybe it’s more of an epic when you take into account the fact that Letters from Iwo Jima is an essential second part to the narrative at hand here. If you watch these two movies together, it'll take you almost exactly four and a half hours, and it'll be a grueling 4.5 hours at that. But that’s definitely an epic, if you treat this double feature like one giant movie, that’s for sure.

Even taking Flags of Our Fathers as one movie, it’s still very ambitious with what it does, and regarding the things it’s willing to explore. It’s like a post-war movie in some ways, digging into the aftermath of a specific battle in some interesting ways. It’s not as focused on the aftermath of World War II to the same extent as something like The Best Days of Our Lives, which is famously all about the aftermath, but the comparison isn't an entirely unfair one to make. Flags of Our Fathers delivers as an anti-war movie as well, both because the combat depicted is effectively savage and intense, and then also with it unpacking trauma and the lingering effects of war for those who survived (in that sense, it scratches a similar itch to the brutally downbeat second half of The Deer Hunter).

Okay, if there’s an opportunity to rave about Letters from Iwo Jima, it’s going to be seized. Sorry, it’s hijacking things. Letters from Iwo Jima is phenomenal. It’s focused on the same battle that Flags of Our Fathers is concerned with, but from the Japanese perspective, and there’s a greater focus on the lead-up to the battle, in contrast to Flags of Our Fathers and its emphasis on the aftermath. That whole aftermath for the Japanese side of the conflict isn't ignored entirely, but since Letters from Iwo Jima is about the side that lost, there obviously isn't as much ground to cover with what happens following the Battle of Iwo Jima.

If you watch Flags of Our Fathers first, you're likely to be impressed, but then if you tackle Letters from Iwo Jima second, you'll be blown away. Also, it’s important to consider the fact that the latter movie does make the former movie even easier to appreciate. They're two sides of the same coin, and though there isn't a catchy name for this particular duology, you're letting yourself down if you watch one without also watching the other. They represent some of the best work Clint Eastwood’s ever done as a director, and the 20-ish years since the pair first came out have done almost nothing to take away from the powerful emotional punch both movies (together) ultimately deliver.

#3501. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3500. John Carpenter’s Involvement In Zack Snyder’s New Sci-Fi Remake Officially Confirmed

John Carpenter will return to help Zack Snyder Escape from New York.

Co-written and directed by the horror icon, the 1981 sci-fi action film starred Kurt Russell as Snake Plissken, a former war hero-turned-criminal who is tasked by the government to rescue the United States President from the island of Manhattan, which has been converted into a maximum security prison in the film's dystopian future setting. Also starring Lee Van Clef, Ernest Borgnine, Isaac Hayes and Adrienne Barbeau, Escape from New York scored favorable reviews from critics and was a box office hit, earning both a 1996 sequel and now a remake from Snyder.

During a recent appearance on Brent Spiner and Jonathan Frakes' Dropping Names podcast, Carpenter offered a brief update on Snyder's Escape from New York. The original writer/director, who is already confirmed to be an executive producer on the project, humorously revealed that he "demanded to be the composer" for the new sci-fi action remake, while also confirming that the production is "not going to use my [original] score," but that instead he and his team are "going to remake the score" from his 1981 film.

Snyder's Escape from New York marks the latest in a string of attempts to bring the sci-fi franchise back to life going back nearly 20 years. Prior plans for the film have included everything from full-on remakes with new actors taking on the role of Snake, including Gerard Butler, while others were meant to instead be legacy sequels much in the way of 2018's Halloween. Prior to the former DC filmmaker, the movie also had everyone from Len Wiseman to Robert Rodriguez, Leigh Whannell and Radio Silence attached to direct.

Interestingly, should the film properly get off the ground, Escape from New York will also mark Snyder's first major venture back into the remake subgenre. The filmmaker memorably got his start with the James Gunn-penned remake of Dawn of the Dead, which was a critical and commercial hit and helped pave the way for his work on everything from 300 to the DC Extended Universe and his Army of the Dead franchise at Netflix.

Carpenter's push to be the composer for the Escape from New York remake certainly shouldn't come as too much of a surprise. Across his 21 feature films in the director's chair, only six did not have Carpenter take on composing duties, with one of the most notable being The Thing, in which he enlisted The Good, the Bad and the Ugly's Ennio Morricone, though he still ended up adding in some of his own music.

It also nicely follows in the footsteps of David Gordon Green's Halloween sequel trilogy, in which Carpenter returned as both an executive producer and composer for all three films. Moreover, the filmmaker collaborated with his son, Cody Carpenter, and Daniel Davies, with their approach being a mix of updating tracks from the original 1978 Halloween as well as bringing a new set of energetic tracks in order to tap into the different pacing of each installment.

Escape From Earth was supposed to be Kurt Russell's third Snake Plisskin adventure, but the disappointment of the second movie ruined that plan.

With Carpenter confirmed for both an EP and composer role on the film, the question now becomes just how much Snyder will look to engage with his predecessor in putting together Escape from New York's script. Snyder has yet to write any of his films alone, generally partnering with Chris Terrio or Kurt Johnstad, and should he enlist input from Carpenter, it could make for a unique melding of the minds to bring a fresh take to Snake Plissken's journey.

Escape from New York is set in a dystopian future where Manhattan serves as a maximum-security prison. The narrative follows a former soldier sent on a perilous mission to rescue the President, who has crash-landed and been captured by the island's inmates.

#3499. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3498. How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

“That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

“When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

For Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

“The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford said, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

#3497. Alan Ritchson’s ‘Reacher’ Is Officially Prime Video’s Most-Watched Show of 2026

2026 has been a benchmark year for Alan Ritchson, who has truly come into his own as one of the biggest action stars in the world right now. Back in March, Ritchson made his Netflix debut in War Machine, the big-budget sci-fi thriller that went on to earn over 135 million views during its first 90 days on streaming. Not only was this enough to pass other movies, such as The Gray Man, to earn a spot as one of the top 10 most-watched Netflix movies ever, but Netflix has also confirmed that a sequel to the film titled War Machines is officially in the works with Ritchson confirmed to return. Later in the year, Ritchson also starred in other films such as Motor City and Runner, which underwhelmed at the box office but have since found success on streaming.

For Ritchson, all of his newfound stardom can be traced back to Prime Video's decision to cast him in the lead role in Reacher, the hit series based on the novels by Lee Child. As the show has continued to pick up more viewers throughout its four season, Ritchson has become more and more popular, which has opened the door for him to star in plenty of other big-budget projects.

Back in August, Prime Video finally released the highly anticipated fourth season of Reacher, but there was little to no doubt that the show was going to be a smash hit. It was renewed for Season 5 months before the Season 4 premiere. After continuing a run of streaming success weeks beyond its Season 4 finale, Alan Ritchson's Reacher has officially become Prime Video's most-watched show of 2026.

Prime Video has yet to announce when Reacher Season 5 will be released, but with production on the new season set to wrap any day now, it's all but confirmed that it will premiere before the end of 2027. The next season will be based on the Jack Reacher novel, Make Me, which is the 20th book in the series. Reacher has also already been picked up for Season 6, but there's no word yet on which book the sixth season will adapt. Even Reacher's flagship spin-off, Neagley, has also been picked up for a second season.

Check out the first four seasons of Reacher on Prime Video and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Alan Ritchson's future projects.

When retired Military Police Officer Jack Reacher is arrested for a murder he did not commit, he finds himself in the middle of a deadly conspiracy full of dirty cops, shady businessmen and scheming politicians. With nothing but his wits, he must figure out what is happening in Margrave, Georgia. The first season of Reacher is based on the international bestseller The Killing Floor by Lee Child.
