#3490. Casting Two & A Half Men Today: 7 Perfect Actors

Two and a Half Men dominated CBS's primetime lineup in the 2000s. The show ran for 12 seasons, and its success also cemented Chuck Lorre as one of television's most influential sitcom creators, helping pave the way for his next CBS hit, The Big Bang Theory.

The premise of Two and a Half Men is simple: a wealthy, womanizing bachelor reluctantly takes in his recently divorced brother and young nephew. What made the sitcom so successful was the chemistry among the cast, and their ability to elevate familiar sitcom archetypes into unforgettable characters.

Charlie Sheen essentially played a heightened version of his own public persona, while Jon Cryer's neurotic, perpetually unlucky Alan provided the perfect foil. Meanwhile, Holland Taylor, Conchata Ferrell, and Melanie Lynskey brought distinct comedic sensibilities to the supporting cast, often stealing scenes from the show's leading men.

Of course, not everything about Two and a Half Men has aged gracefully, particularly its treatment of women. However, the central premise of two dysfunctional brothers with completely incompatible lifestyles sharing a home remains ripe for reinvention. A contemporary recasting should find performers who can bring their own comedic identities to these seven memorable characters.

Charlie Harper was written for Charlie Sheen, whose reputation as a Hollywood bad boy informed the character before Two and a Half Men even premiered. Audiences were already familiar with Sheen's hard-partying lifestyle, high-profile relationships, and tabloid scandals, allowing the sitcom to establish Charlie's womanizing ways without an extensive backstory.

Much of the character's humor depended on viewers recognizing the similarities between the fictional bachelor and the actor playing him. Consequently, recasting Charlie Harper requires more than finding an actor with comedic talent. Dylan O'Brien has the acting chops and enough romantic turmoil in his public history to make an interesting choice.

Joe Jonas could easily play a former musician living off royalties. Unfortunately, Jonas being one of three famous brothers would make the premise of Two and a Half Men a little harder to sell. Pete Davidson, however, is the closest modern equivalent to Sheen.

Between his high-profile relationships and his history of partying and substance use, Davidson has developed a public persona that audiences already associate with Charlie Harper's lifestyle. Davidson's best projects have also demonstrated a willingness to mine his personal struggles and tabloid reputation for laughs, particularly in The King of Staten Island and Bupkis.

His self-deprecating humor and perpetually disheveled charm could make Charlie's irresponsible lifestyle strangely endearing. At the same time, his past provides the same built-in backstory that made Sheen's casting so effective.

Alan Harper is the uptight foil to Charlie's hedonistic lifestyle. The financially struggling chiropractor is neurotic, insecure, and self-righteous, but his desperation for approval often makes him just as ridiculous as Charlie. Fortunately, plenty of contemporary actors could tackle this familiar sitcom archetype.

Ben Platt has practically perfected playing uptight characters, while Daniel Radcliffe's work in Miracle Workers demonstrates his ability to embrace absurd desperation. Jack Quaid, meanwhile, has made a career out of playing overwhelmed everymen surrounded by increasingly outrageous personalities.

However, Superbad actor Christopher Mintz-Plasse has the awkward comedic timing and ability to play the desperate need to appear cool that would make Alan's constant humiliations particularly entertaining. Much like Jon Cryer, who was best known for playing Duckie in Pretty in Pink before Two and a Half Men, Mintz-Plasse became famous playing an awkward teenager with the famous McLovin fake ID in Superbad.

Opposite Pete Davidson's effortlessly charismatic Charlie, Mintz-Plasse could play Alan as a man who desperately wants his brother's lifestyle but lacks the confidence or social skills to pull it off. Like Cryer in 2003, he'd transform an iconic teenage comedy persona into an adult who still hasn't figured out how to be cool.

Alts: Ben Platt, Daniel Radcliffe, Jack Quaid

Casting child actors is always something of a gamble, particularly for a sitcom that could potentially run for several seasons. Fortunately, Two and a Half Men would have an ensemble of established comedic performers to carry the show while its youngest cast member finds his footing.

Angus T. Jones was a relative unknown when the original series premiered in 2003, and a modern reboot would benefit from taking a similar approach rather than relying on an established child star. Evan Wen, a young actor with a handful of commercials and short-film credits, could be an interesting choice for Jake Harper.

Beyond acting, Wen has a variety of interests, including hip-hop, playing the trombone, and fencing, suggesting a well-rounded young performer whose personality could help shape the character. After all, Jake's appeal comes from his natural, unfiltered reactions to the dysfunctional adults around him, rather than delivering overly slick punchlines.

With Christopher Mintz-Plasse as Alan and Constance Wu as Judith, the writers could incorporate elements of both parents' personalities while tailoring Jake's interests and comedic sensibilities to Wen's strengths. A reboot could improve Jake's ending in Two and a Half Men and allow a promising newcomer to grow into the role and make Jake his own.

Evelyn Harper is an arch sitcom character: a wealthy, sharp-tongued, sexually liberated mother who cares far more about her own pleasures than her children's well-being. Essentially an older, female version of Charlie, Evelyn routinely criticizes both sons, particularly Alan, while demonstrating little genuine maternal warmth.

Holland Taylor brought an air of sophistication, drawing on her established talent for playing intimidating, chic women who could eviscerate someone with a single remark. Many actresses could follow in Taylor's footsteps. Jean Smart played a similar character as Deborah Vance in Hacks, Jennifer Coolidge could bring a more eccentric sensibility, and Jane Krakowski has mastered playing glamorous, narcissistic women.

However, Megan Mullally feels practically destined to inherit the role. Mullally's Karen Walker from Will & Grace is essentially Evelyn turned up to eleven: a wealthy, self-indulgent woman with an insatiable appetite for alcohol, sex, and insulting everyone around her.

Mullally has the distinctive voice, impeccable sitcom timing, and unapologetic sexual confidence to make Evelyn's cruelty hilarious. More importantly, she can deliver a devastating insult that only makes the audience love her more, ensuring Evelyn remains entertaining even when she's being an absolutely terrible mother.

Alts: Jean Smart, Jennifer Coolidge, Jane Krakowski

Judith Harper-Melnick is Alan's bitter, controlling ex-wife, who seems to exist to make his life miserable. However, the joke in Two and a Half Men is that Alan is often just as insufferable as Judith. Both are anxious, controlling, and convinced they're the reasonable person in every argument.

Their similarities help explain why their marriage failed, as neither can let anything go, and both are exceptionally talented at making the other feel terrible. Unlike the show's more outrageous personalities, Judith is a relatively straight character whose comedy comes from her exasperation and passive-aggressive exchanges with Alan.

Marin Hinkle excelled at making Judith simultaneously sympathetic and infuriating. Brenda Song could certainly play a high-strung suburban mother, but Constance Wu is an especially natural fit. As Jessica Huang in Fresh Off the Boat, Wu demonstrated her ability to play a fiercely opinionated mother whose determination to control everything frequently backfires.

Wu can make even the most unreasonable behavior feel completely justified from her character's perspective. Opposite Christopher Mintz-Plasse's Alan, she could recreate the deliciously dysfunctional dynamic of two people who bring out the absolute worst in each other.

Berta was originally intended to appear in just two episodes of Two and a Half Men, with Charlie's housekeeper quitting after Alan moves in because she can't stand him. However, Conchata Ferrell was so hilarious as the foul-mouthed, intimidating housekeeper that Berta became a staple of the sitcom throughout its 12-season run.

The working-class woman was completely unimpressed by Charlie's wealth and could put him in his place with a single devastating insult. Whoever inherits the role needs to be rough around the edges, effortlessly funny, and intimidating enough to keep Charlie and Alan in line.

The role could be reimagined in many different ways, but Fortune Feimster offers a particularly compelling combination of deadpan delivery and approachable charm. As Colette in The Mindy Project, Feimster showed she can play a blunt, unapologetically unconventional character without making her unlikable.

Her stand-up persona is similarly unpretentious, with a conversational delivery that makes even her most outrageous observations feel completely natural. Rather than imitating Ferrell's gruffness, Feimster could make Berta disarmingly friendly one moment and brutally dismissive the next.

Alts: Niecy Nash-Betts, Wendi McLendon-Covey, Retta, Jenifer Lewis

Played by Melanie Lynskey, Rose is one of the most delightfully unhinged characters in Two and a Half Men. She's Charlie's seemingly sweet, quirky neighbor who is actually an obsessive, manipulative stalker. Lynskey's soft voice, cheerful demeanor, and almost childlike sweetness made Rose's increasingly disturbing behavior hilarious.

Rose is also one of the characters whose original premise has aged the least gracefully, although her underlying comedic potential remains enormous. A modern recasting would benefit from making Rose less of a one-sided stalker and more of a genuinely tempting but toxic romantic prospect Charlie knows he should avoid.

Geraldine Viswanathan and Molly Gordon could both capture Rose's deceptively innocent exterior, but Rachel Sennott would bring a more chaotic, sexually confident energy to the character. In Shiva Baby and Bodies Bodies Bodies, Sennott demonstrated her ability to make deeply uncomfortable situations hilarious while playing impulsive, emotionally volatile characters.

Having already appeared alongside Pete Davidson in Bodies Bodies Bodies, Sennott could establish a similarly unpredictable dynamic with his Charlie in Two and a Half Men. Rather than simply pursuing a man who wants nothing to do with her, Sennott's Rose could be someone Charlie keeps inviting back into his life despite knowing exactly how badly it will end.

Alts: Geraldine Viswanathan, Molly Gordon

#3489. Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI

Machines can automate drudgery but engineers make key decisions

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility.

AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project.

Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty.

Consider a software engineer working on a medical device. AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model.

That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts.

The same is true in energy, transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations.

Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together.

Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs.

AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops.

Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges.

New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood.

In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project.

AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less.

Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People are essential where context, values, responsibility, and judgment matter. The challenge is to decide where each belongs.

An AI system might generate several designs for a medical sensor, for example, and predict how each will perform. An engineer can test the predictions and reject designs that violate technical requirements. A clinician can determine whether the sensor can be realistically used. Patients and practitioners might reveal problems that neither the engineer nor the developer considered. The final solution emerges from combining the perspectives.

The engineer is still a builder and specialist but increasingly also a coordinator of knowledge.

An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project.

The broader form of engineering creates an important role for IEEE. Its societies already bring together expertise in various technologies, engineering education, technical standards, and other fields. That makes IEEE well placed to help engineers work across specialties without weakening the value of specialization.

IEEE could create more communities organized around problems that require expertise from several fields. Examples include trustworthy clinical AI, resilient infrastructure, energy reliability, scientific discovery, and safe autonomous systems. An engineer could begin in a home discipline and then work with specialists from other IEEE communities as a project requires.

IEEE also can help set practical standards for human-machine collaboration. Engineers will need clear guidance on when AI-generated work must be checked, how uncertainty should be documented, when a specialist must make a decision, and who is responsible when a system uses both human judgment and machine output.

Those questions are becoming part of everyday engineering. They should not be left to each company or project manager to answer independently. A professional organization can provide common expectations that follow engineers as they move between jobs, industries, and technical fields.

AI does not make engineering disciplines less important; it makes the connections between them easier to use. Deep expertise gives engineers the foundation to judge what is sound. Systems thinking helps them understand how different parts of a problem fit together. AI can extend engineers’ ability to explore, test, and communicate across fields. Human judgment gives the work direction and responsibility.

An engineer is not defined only by a job title or a fixed set of tasks. An engineer is someone trained to understand complex systems, define and redefine problems, bring together the knowledge and tools needed to solve them, test whether solutions work, and take responsibility for the outcome.

That is what it means to be an “unbound” engineer.

The boundaries between specialties become easier to cross, and machines might take on more of the technical work, but the core of engineering remains human: deciding what problem is worth solving, what evidence is good enough, how the pieces fit together, and what to do when the answer is uncertain.

Sufian Aldogom is an IEEE member, a research affiliate at MIT, and a senior leader at Google in Sunnyvale, Calif.

#3488. How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.]

World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”

How’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” said Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he said. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he said, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”

#3487. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

#3486. Matt Damon’s 172-Minute War Epic Is Officially Returning to Theaters

There should be no doubt that 2026 was the year for movies. Every few months delivered the next big thing, from sci-fi to drama to war movies. One of the most anticipated was The Odyssey, a new feature from Christopher Nolan that may be considered his magnum opus in years to come. Finally dispensing with the dead wife narrative, he wrote an emotionally compelling part for Anne Hathaway while also adapting one of the most famous stories ever told.

One of the biggest hurdles was making Matt Damon’s version of Odysseus palatable for a modern audience. The Odyssey takes huge archetypes and molds them to be relatable and more human than their divine counterparts. Acting, music, and cinematography all came together in a story that is miraculously heading back to theaters. On December 11, fans can relive the horror of war when The Odyssey returns to 10,000 screens in IMAX and IMAX 70mm.

There have been many attempts at adapting The Odyssey before, but none have quite got to the heart of what it means to be human. Though experts were free with the criticism of Christopher Nolan’s interpretation of Homer’s epic poem, the director was free to develop a story that would speak to modern viewers. Many aspects wouldn’t translate; the biggest of all was investing in a belief that Odysseus would really not find a way home for 20 years.

This question is answered in the emotional character arc that takes the Trojan War hero from place to place. One of the best sequences of the film was the infamous invasion of Troy and the iconic horse that comes with it. Sneaking into Troy via a hollow wooden horse was Odysseus’ brainchild, and he becomes traumatized by what his decision wreaked. The scene shows the destruction of the city and the looting and murder that always come with war.

Zendaya’s performance as a priestess who gets beheaded in the siege is one of the most emotional moments of the movie. Odysseus never forgets the lives he was responsible for taking, even if it was indirectly. He feels that he doesn’t deserve to get home because of his crimes, putting a fine point on the PTSD narrative that runs through the film. The Odyssey provides a modern context for viewers to see these characters not as archetypes, but as people.

While Nolan certainly took creative liberties with the material, there is no denying that this is one of the best movies of the decade. The performances from Matt Damon, Zendaya, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, and Tom Holland were a masterclass of acting that comes together in the final act. Even in an age where movie length fatigue is real, not one minute of The Odyssey’s close-to-three-hour runtime is wasted. It all culminates in Odysseus finally accepting that he can come home after the horror of war as well as the loss of his men. The Odyssey will prove to be a modern classic that fans can see once again on the big screen.

#3485. Every The Hunger Games Movie, Ranked From Worst To Best (Including Sunrise On The Reaping)

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping's release shakes up the ranking of all The Hunger Games movies from worst to best, as they aren't all of equal quality. Lionsgate brought Suzanne Collins' best-selling YA dystopian sci-fi series to the big screen in 2012, just four years after the first book. Since then, audiences have been treated to six movies following a few different protagonists.

The action-packed but socially relevant films about fighting back against oppressive regimes began with a focus on Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence), as she enters the 74th Hunger Games, becomes the symbol of a rebellion against the Capitol and President Snow (Donald Sutherland), and navigates her feelings for Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson) and Gale Hawthorne (Liam Hemsworth). These three, along with Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson), were at the heart of the first four blockbusters.

Given the popularity of the Hunger Games movies, Collins wrote prequel books that Lionsgate was quick to turn into movies themselves. The first made Snow the main character, as The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes showed him mentoring Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), District 12's female tribute in the 10th Hunger Games. Sunrise on the Reaping brought a younger Haymitch (Joseph Zada) into the spotlight to show his participation in the 50th Hunger Games.

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 1 (2014)

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2 (2015)

The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023)

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (2026)

All six Hunger Games movies have been positively received by critics and general audiences, which has only made it tougher for many to rank them. With some aging better or worse and new entries like Sunrise on the Reaping coming, the whole franchise ranking shifts.

On the heels of the first two films' success, Lionsgate elected to split Collins' final book in the Katniss trilogy into two parts. This was always viewed as a risky decision, especially since the first half is very different from what came before. Mockingjay Part 1 is stripped of any real interactions between Katniss and Peeta, and shifts the setting from the arena to the war-torn Districts.

The result is a movie that hinges much more on Katniss and Gale's relationship, which was fairly underdeveloped in the previous installments. Lawrence and Hemsworth's chemistry is fine, but it isn't strong enough to support the film. Katniss (and the movie) misses Peeta's optimism and charm desperately.

Katniss' arc of accepting her role as the Mockingjay is effective, and there are a few solid set pieces as she explores other Districts. However, Mockingjay Part 1 never shakes the feeling that it is stretching out the franchise's conclusion for an easy cash grab. The result is the stakes feeling very low, as no major characters die, with all casualties coming in the form of nameless citizens.

Mockingjay Part 2 was a low point for the franchise in terms of general interest and reception, but the movie has held up better than its predecessor. It leans back into the blockbuster spectacle that the franchise conditioned audiences to expect. Katniss and her team navigating a booby-trapped Capitol allows the film to deliver some exciting and fresh life-or-death situations, with mostly effective deaths.

Coin's death is the most satisfying of them all, as Katniss rids the world of another potential dictator ready to spill children's blood to incite fear. That decision, paired with her getting a peaceful life with Peeta and their children, makes for a great conclusion to her story.

Ultimately, Mockingjay Part 2 is a solid, thrilling conclusion to Katniss' saga. There is a fresh layer of tension to her and Peeta's dynamic that slowly fades throughout the movie, showing just how strong their relationship really is. It might fly through some major moments and become too dark at times, but its action and strong performances across the board help.

After Katniss' story ended, there was not a huge push to see Snow's origin story. The evil, poison-loving ruler of Panem was hardly a character people would cite as someone they wanted to spend more time with. Yet, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes proved that there was much more to explore in his teenage years to explore how he rose to power.

Remarkably, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes does its job of making audiences care about Snow and understand (but not necessarily relate to) why he became a charming, ruthless ruler. Seeing the tough conditions of Snow's earlier years is effective, while he is humanized by introducing Lucy Gray Baird, the District 12 tribute who wins the 10th Hunger Games with Snow as her mentor.

Their dynamic is why the movie works, with Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler selling the unexpected romance. They have better chemistry than Lawrence and Hemsworth in Mockingjay Part 1, even if the movie is also lacking in action overall. It goes above Mockingjay Part 2 thanks to having better, more developed characters and relationships.

Sunrise on the Reaping is the prequel fans wanted for years. Haymitch's games have been a point of interest ever since Catching Fire's book, and now we have seen just how captivating and devastating his origin really was. Anchored by a strong cast, epic action, and a lot of franchise connections, Sunrise on the Reaping becomes an invaluable entry.

Joseph Zada does a fairly great job of becoming a believably younger version of Woody Harrelson's character, giving him the same wit, protective spirit, and edges. Seeing him compete in the 50th Hunger Games and become part of an early rebellion plot is incredibly exciting, with the film really making you care about what happens to him and other tributes, even though its prequel status means some of this is already well-known.

Sunrise on the Reaping is bolstered by stellar supporting cast members in Mckenna Grace, Whitney Peak, Jesse Plemons, Glenn Close, and more. Book purists will ultimately be disappointed by a few notable scenes that were cut and how those change the story, while some of the returning characters come across as more forced than natural. All in all, it strikes a better balance of its characters, action, emotionality, and themes than the films ranked lower.

The Hunger Games launched the franchise in a terrific fashion. The movie wastes little time endearing Katniss to audiences, ensuring that we care about her from the moment she volunteers in Prim's place until the 74th Hunger Games are over. Lawrence immediately embodies the character from Collins' books, giving her all the resilience and compassion expected from the strong-willed District 12 teenager.

Since The Hunger Games was not yet a proven franchise, there is a slightly more grounded approach applied by director Gary Ross. His action is more brutal and frenetic, which adds to the feeling of experiencing what it's like in the arena for the first time. The less polished look feels right for District 12 and seeing the whole experience through Katniss' eyes.

The movie, and its Games, hinge on accepting there is a genuine connection between Katniss and Peeta, and Lawrence and Hutcherson do their part to make it work. Harrelson and Elizabeth Banks' Effie nearly steal the whole show, while Amandla Stenberg's Rue adds a wonderful (and heartbreaking) dynamic with Katniss. The Hunger Games set a very high bar for everything that came after.

For as great as the original is, Catching Fire took the Hunger Games franchise to new heights that still have yet to be eclipsed. Director Francis Lawrence steps aboard to level up the action and scale, which is very fitting given the stakes of the 3rd Quarter Quell. Everything from the characters, performances, action, sets, and visuals stands above every other entry in the series.

The personal stakes are clear for Katniss even before the Games begin, thanks to showing what her life has become in 12 after the win. Once the tributes enter the franchise's best arena, the unique dangers and setup elevate things further. Katniss and Peeta's relationship is once again key to it all, but Finnick, Johanna, Beetee, and Plutarch are excellent new additions to the world. They each feel fully realized no matter how big or small their presence really is.

Ultimately, Catching Fire is a perfect fusion of blockbuster action and YA romance. The faked love between Katniss and Peeta becomes real and believable thanks to sequences like Peeta's near-death experience or their talk on the beach. The action is impeccable, and the stakes that come with it are about as high as the franchise can go. Add in the surprise conclusion of the 75th Hunger Games for any non-book readers (or how well executed the plot is for those in the know), and there's no doubt this is the best The Hunger Games movie from start to finish.

#3484. ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

#3482. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3480. How Walton Goggins' New Fantasy Movie "Redefines" Classic 63-Year-Old Disney Story Tradition

EXCLUSIVE: Disney's upcoming fantasy movie Hexed is putting a new spin on one of the studio's oldest storytelling traditions.

Disney has explored the idea of a "Chosen One" for decades, dating back to one of the earliest King Arthur movies, 1963's The Sword in the Stone, which follows a young Arthur before he becomes king. The theme has since appeared in movies such as Moana, where the titular heroine is chosen by the ocean to restore the heart of Te Fiti. However, Disney's latest animated adventure is taking a different approach to what makes someone special.

Directed by Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand, Hexed follows Billie (Hailee Steinfeld), an unconventional teenager who discovers she has magical abilities. After being transported to a hidden world of witches, she must work alongside her mother, Alice (Rashida Jones), to uncover family secrets. The voice cast also includes Walton Goggins as a magical three-eyed cat named Beef Roger Crummchuk and Jodie Foster as Queen Celeste.

In an interview with ScreenRant's Kim Horcher, Disney Animation Chief Creative Officer and Hexed co-writer Jared Bush explained how the upcoming movie redefines the traditional "Chosen One" narrative. Bush revealed that the filmmakers wanted magic to represent personal potential, rather than simply making one character more important than everyone else. Read his comments below:

Yeah, it's a few different reasons, honestly. We really wanted to make sure that we knew what magic was supposed to represent. And in this film, it's really a metaphor for our own potential, or our spark. I think something that was important to all of us is to say that sometimes you know what that is right away, and sometimes it takes time. Sometimes it actually takes someone seeing that in you and helping bring that out of you. And that's really what the story is about.

I think for this film, the idea that there is a Chosen One, and you get to uncover that throughout the story, is a really exciting thing. Obviously, Disney has this great legacy. Moana is a great example of a character you think is going to be the Chosen One who goes out into this world. I think that we wanted to both lean into that legacy, but also redefine it in this film.

I'm glad you said that. That was the whole point, and it frankly took a lot of work to try to get that right.

During an early press event, the Hexed movie trailer offered a glimpse at Billie's journey and her complicated relationship with her mother, Alice. The footage highlighted the mother-daughter dynamic at the center of the story, which connects to Bush's comments about discovering one's potential.

Disney has explored the "Chosen One" in movies such as Hercules, where the titular hero must prove himself worthy of becoming a god, and Encanto, where Mirabel struggles to find her place in a family gifted with magical abilities. However, Hexed takes a different approach, focusing on how someone's potential may not be immediately obvious and sometimes requires others' encouragement to be discovered.

This approach also connects to the mother-daughter dynamic between Billie and Alice, which is central to the story. As the mother and daughter navigate the magical world together, their journey could help Billie better understand both her abilities and herself.

With Disney continuing to remake familiar stories and characters, Hexed offers an opportunity to introduce a new kind of hero. While the movie draws inspiration from the studio's animated classics, Bush's comments suggest that its approach to the "Chosen One" storyline could set it apart from previous Disney adventures.

Hexed arrives in theaters on November 25, 2026.

#3478. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3477. Ridley Scott's Involvement In New Blade Runner Series Clarified By Showrunner & EPs

Ahead of Blade Runner 2099's official release, executive producers Silka Louisa and Broderick Johnson revealed the extent to which franchise creator Ridley Scott was involved with the Prime Video series.

Set 50 years after Blade Runner 2049, the show stars Hunter Schafer as Cora, a human pretending to be a replicant, and Michelle Yeoh as Olwen, an aging replicant, in a world where replicants are dominant over humans. The rest of the cast is rounded out by Dimitri Abold and Lewis Gribben.

In an interview with Maude Garrett for ScreenRant, the Blade Runner 2099 executive producers addressed working with Scott on one of his most iconic properties. "It's a dream come true to know all of the secrets and ask him all the questions and find out what everything really means," Louisa said.

However, she clarify that some secrets have to stay close to her chest. "The one thing I don't tell anyone because, I will warn you, you think you want to know, but you don't want to know," the writer explained. "The power of never really being sure, the ambiguity is that, is so tantalizing. And somebody actually just telling you definitively, "It's X, it's Y..." It just kind of neuters the magic trick." A key factor in Blade Runner's appeal over the decades has been its ambiguity over whether Rick Deckard (portrayed by Harrison Ford in Scott's Blade Runner) is himself a replicant, a question Louisa sidesteps because "everyone tries" to get a solid answer from her.

For Johnson, his working relationship with Scott goes back "now a good 15 years," and he still recalls the open attitude the filmmaker had to expanding the world of Blade Runner. "When we first got the IP and went and sat with him," said Johnson. "He told us in that first meeting that Blade Runner was never meant to be a one-off exercise, which we were thrilled to hear. That collaboration has gone on since then."

According to Johnson, Scott's collaborative approach very much extended to Louisa's vision for Blade Runner 2099. "He responded to Silka's original idea very positively as well," he continued. "He's been a part of that iteration from the [start], deciding whether it's a hundred years or it's 50 years or whatever. He was part of that whole thing, dreaming with her at that point, down to giving notes on the edits and whatnot."

Scott himself previously discussed his involvement with the series, somewhat contradicting the assertion he was heavily involved. "I can’t blame my lawyers and my agents at that time, but somehow we let ‘Blade Runner’ go," he said earlier this year. "And when you’re not the author of the actual written word, you don’t have a piece."

Blade Runner 2099 debuts on Prime Video on November 25, 2026.

#3476. The 8 Most Challenging Books To Read That Are 100% Worth It

Many things can make a book challenging to read. Perhaps it's because their use of language is deliberately labyrinthine or jargon-heavy, because their narrative structure feels almost surreal, or because a lot of background knowledge is required to fully understand the story. In any case, there have been innumerable great-yet-difficult books written over the years, and it just so happens that quite a few of them are among the best books ever written.

From foundational classics like In Search of Lost Time to modern award-winning masterpieces like Angel Down, these are books which are certainly challenging to get through, but are so phenomenal that they are 100% worth the challenge. For the purposes of this list, only books that were specifically designed to be challenging will be considered, rather than great books that are hard to read today mostly because they have dated aspects, which is a whole other topic. The entries are ranked by a mixture of how essential and how challenging each book is.

French novelist, essayist, and literary critic Marvel Proust was one of the most influential authors of the entire 20th century, best-known for his seven-volume magnum opus In Search of Lost Time. Published between 1913 and 1927, the novel is composed of a narrator's recollections of his childhood and journey to adulthood, revisiting his past, romantic obsessions, and relationships with French high society as he tries to find his purpose as a writer.

The main reason why In Search of Lost Time is such a challenging read goes without saying. Depending on what format one reads it in, the novel is over 4,000 pages and 1.2 million words long. It's a kind of literary Everest that many a bibliophile considers a true goal to climb to the top, and far from being a tedious journey that's mostly worth reading just because it's a classic, it's a genuinely phenomenal work of art of tremendous psychological depth and gorgeous prose.

Toni Morrison's Beloved is one of those books that everyone should read before kicking the bucket, one of the most consequential American novels of the 20th century. It tells the story of a formerly enslaved mother in post-Civil War Ohio, as she's haunted by the ghost of the baby she killed to spare her from slavery. The book won the 1988 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction and is still widely remembered as one of the most foundational texts for postcolonial, African American, and feminist literature.

On the one hand, you have the book's brutally harrowing subject matter, which Morrison dives deep into without flinching at any point. On top of that, you get the highly fragmented, non-linear storytelling, as well as Morrison's dense and poetic prose. But though it isn't an easy read, Beloved is absolutely breathtaking, a book whose historical importance is matched only by its artistic quality.

Though the world of Latin American literature hasn't been quite as internationally mainstream throughout the 21st century as it was during the '60s and '70s, it has nonetheless delivered several incredible masterpieces. Case in point: Chilean writer Roberto Bolaño's postmodern meta-novel 2666, a gut-wrenching tale about four European literary critics searching for an elusive German author. On their journey, they encounter a wave of unsolved femicides in a Mexican border town inspired by Ciudad Juárez.

2666 is nothing but relentless surrealist cruelty over a whopping 900 pages, easily making it one of the heaviest books of all time. Reading it requires not only deciphering its sprawling, fragmented structure, but also bearing such a devastatingly realistic depiction of violence toward women in Mexico and Latin America that getting to the end of the novel is already an achievement in itself. But far from feeling exploitative, 2666 is propelled by Bolaño's hypnotic prose and unforgettable characters, making all of the bleakness worth every word.

Legendary postmodernist icon Thomas Pynchon was well-known for writing some of the densest, most complex and challenging novels of the entire postmodern movement, such as the satirical historical sci-fi masterpiece Gravity's Rainbow. It's one of the heaviest sci-fi books ever written, about an American soldier fighting in Europe during World War II. There, he discovers that his sexual encounters map onto future German rocket strikes, launching a paranoid quest into a secret conspiracy.

Generally considered Pynchon's most deliberately challenging novel, Gravity's Rainbow stands as a total refusal of traditional ideas of narrative. There's no conventional plot, no real character arc, no linear time; instead, the whole book is overloaded with theology, history, economics, pop culture references, and labyrinthine language. Even so, Gravity's Rainbow is a must-read for people already familiar with Pynchon's style, since it very well may be the quintessential countercultural epic.

Plenty of great books have won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction throughout the 2020s, and Daniel Kraus' Angel Down is one of the best. In it, World War I soldiers venture into No Man's Land to put a wounded comrade out of his misery, only to find a fallen angel whose fate plants greed, paranoia, and moral ruin in their midst. It already seems like a compelling enough premise on paper, but what really makes Angel Down so special—and so challenging—is that the whole thing is a single unbroken sentence.

Making a single sentence span a whopping 300 pages was always going to be a gargantuan task to complete successfully, but Angel Down really does live up to the hype. Yes, the complete lack of breaks in the book is mentally draining, but it's worth every bit of effort it demands. Angel Down is a deeply moving and thought-provoking study of the existential horrors of war, blending visceral supernatural horror and war thriller genre elements faultlessly.

One of the most important and influential American writers of his generation, William Faulkner is still considered one of the spearheads of 20th-century Southern American literature and modernist fiction. In his fourth-ever novel, he delivered his magnum opus. The Sound and the Fury chronicles the collapse of an aristocratic Mississippi family as three brothers' obsessions with their sister unravel across fragmented, shifting perspectives.

The result of such a premise is one of those perfect books that immediately demand a re-read, and that speaks both to this masterpiece's tremendous quality and highly challenging stream-of-consciousness style. The Sound and the Fury feels like one of the most successful experiments that modernist fiction ever gave us, shifting through several different perspectives that make the whole reading experience feel like a psychological maze. Getting through it, however, delivers one of the most foundational masterpieces of early-20th-century American literature.

"New sincerity" was a trend in late-20th-century art that sought to break away from postmodernism's sense of irony and cynicism, in relation to the post-postmodern cultural paradigm of metamodernism. As far as those concepts go, you can't really get many exponents much better than David Foster Wallace's magnum opus, Infinite Jest. Cataloged as an encyclopedic novel, it's set in a near-future North America where Quebec separatists, intelligence agents, tennis prodigies, and recovering addicts collide in a search for a fatally addictive film cartridge created by a late filmmaker.

The result is one of the most ambitious books of all time, a 1,000-page doorstop that serves as a potent statement about addiction, entertainment, isolation, and the endless search for sincere human connection. It's a towering artistic achievement packed with hundreds of endnotes with vital information, a challenging non-linear structure, and hyper-dense prose that makes reading multiple pages at a time all that much harder. However, it's also a brilliantly prophetic satire about entertainment and the media, full of hilarious set pieces and intelligent payoffs.

One of the most influential and groundbreaking writers of the 20th century, James Joyce wrote what many would consider a remarkably strong contender for the elusive title of The Great American Novel: Ulysses, one of the classics that belong on everyone's bucket list. This is a modernist mirror of Homer's Odyssey, following an ordinary Dublin advertiser and a young writer through a single day in their ordinary lives. Who could have possibly predicted that a book that simply narrates a mundane day could be so challenging?

Indeed, Joyce completely reinvents the rules that his book operates under with practically every single chapter, writing in an unfiltered stream of consciousness that never holds the reader's hand. Full of dense allusions to things like Catholic theology, Shakespearean scholarship, and Dublin lore, it's certainly not an easy masterpiece to get through, but it's a must-read nonetheless. But as challenging as it is, Ulysses is also the most admirable and humane portrait of an ordinary person ever written as fiction, an absolute masterwork that belongs on the bookshelf of everyone who loves books.

#3475. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

If you're having trouble accessing your bank right now, you aren't alone. As of Monday afternoon, a number of banks are experiencing outages and interruptions to service.
