#3473. ‘Rosemary’s Baby’ Meets ‘The Fly’ in a New Body Horror Thriller Officially Out Now

Hannah covers horror, sci-fi, and games at Collider, where she writes news and features, reviews new releases, and interviews the people who make them. She’s helping build out Collider’s gaming coverage, with Pokémon as one of her specialties. If she isn’t writing about a monster, she’s probably watching one on a tape from her VHS collection.

Nora Pacetti figures her daughter is teething. It would explain the screaming, and by bath time, Olivia seems happy enough. There’s still the matter of what looks like a splinter in her arm, though Nora can’t think where a baby would have picked one up. Her mother, Giulia, gets a good look while she’s toweling off her granddaughter and asks Nora to run downstairs for her reading glasses. Of all the things a grandmother might find on a changing table, an incoming feather takes some explaining.

Giulia is usually the person Nora can count on to have whatever a child might need. She carries an ice pack in her purse in case somebody else’s kid takes a fall, and she also spends enough time watching conspiracy videos on YouTube that Nora would like a second opinion on the feather. Her husband is happy to oblige. He wants to take Olivia to a specialist, and under almost any other circumstances, Nora would probably be the one making the appointment. This time, she’s afraid of what might happen once somebody else gets a look at her daughter.

Christina Henry’s Pinfeathers is out now from Berkley. Released November 17, the 320-page thriller is the 20th book from the author of The Place Where They Buried Your Heart. The book has already drawn comparisons to both Rosemary’s Baby and David Cronenberg’s The Fly, with the feathers accounting for the Cronenberg half. The Rosemary’s Baby bit comes into play when people outside the family begin asking questions about Olivia, and Nora has to figure out who told them enough to ask.

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

Henry told the Chicago Sun-Times that the image of a baby sprouting feathers came to her before she knew the story. She begins her books in longhand and works out what those early images mean as she writes. In this case, that process brought her to a new mother in a condo on Chicago’s North Side. Henry described the fear behind Nora’s story as “the parental anxiety around illness, difficulty, things that you don’t expect when you become a parent.”

Readers can get a look at the scene that started it all in an excerpt published by The Nerd Daily, which shows the three generations of Pacetti women in the middle of an otherwise ordinary visit. Giulia shows up with food, kisses her daughter hello, and nudges her out of the way so she can have a turn with the baby. By the time she notices Olivia’s arm, Henry has already established who usually takes charge in this family.

Pinfeathers is available now in hardcover, ebook, and audiobook.

#3472. 10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?)

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

An isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

One of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

If you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

If you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

If your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

If you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous new reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

If you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

There is something charming about the crunch of gravel underfoot, and whether you are aiming for a relaxed rustic country look or strong architectural lines in a contemporary yard, gravel has a place in both.

I’m a huge fan of gravel and the small stones in my front and backyard — in fact, I’m even considering digging up most of my lawn next year to plant a dry garden — an approach that makes gravel even more central to the space.

Unfortunately, keeping gravel spotless can be a chore. Pesky weeds have a way of popping up and disturbing the landscaping. But it doesn’t have to be this way. With the right prep work and a few weed-removal tricks, if they do sprout up, you can enjoy the look without backbreaking weeding.

While gravel might seem far less hospitable to weeds than bare soil, they still manage to find a way. Wind, birds, and nearby plants constantly drop seeds between the stones, while fallen leaves and grass clippings gradually break down — creating just enough organic matter and moisture for those seeds to take root.

But weeds can also take root from below if the ground wasn’t prepared properly before the stones were laid.

The key to achieving a beautiful expanse of gravel, without a weed in sight, is to get the basics right.

Extensive ground prep ahead of time is really going to be the part that saves you the biggest headaches when putting down gravel

Dawn DeFeo, head of landscaping & gardening at Landscape Barn, confirms, “Extensive ground prep ahead of time is really going to be the part that saves you the biggest headaches when putting down gravel.”

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

So what exactly does this involve? DeFeo says you need to start by removing any weeds and roots that are already there. And I know from experience that if you skip this step, you are already in trouble.

Once you’ve prepared the ground and removed any offending weeds, she recommends covering the base area with landscaping fabric, and adds, “Make sure you overlap a bit to stop new weeds from sneaking up through the seams.”

You might be wondering whether you need to lay down sand before placing the landscaping fabric, but DeFeo isn’t a fan. “A lot of people recommend it, but I’d skip the sand. It can actually work against you; weeds seem to like growing in it.”

I have two different types of gravel in my yard: a large white stone covers a small space in my front yard, and I’ve laid finer pea gravel in my backyard. Both have fabric landscaping underneath that keeps most weeds at bay.

But what does DeFeo recommend? “Crushed gravel around a half inch does a good job fitting together as opposed to the smoother, rounder stuff,” says DeFeo. “Just make sure to get a good three to four inches down so you can’t see any of your fabric.”

These garden gloves are made of nylon and nitrile and come in three sizes — small, medium and large. They offer excellent non-slip properties, are comfortable around the wrist, breathable and machine washable. At Tom's Guide, we recommend them as the best overall gardening glove.

Despite getting the groundwork right and laying a landscaping fabric and choosing stones that sit tightly together to stop seeds from penetrating, some weeds will still peek through.

Gillian Metetansky, founder of The Southern Garden Edit, explains why it’s not a foolproof method, “Weeds can still come via the wind blowing the seeds or through wildlife like birds spreading them.”

There’s not much you can do to prevent nature from doing its thing, but by getting the groundwork right, it will be easier to keep on top of the weeds that do appear.

Weed patrolSo, what is the best method to remove weeds from gravel? “I only recommend removing weeds by using a vinegar spray and pulling them up from the base,” explains Metetansky.

Besides using the vinegar spray to remove weeds and pulling, she warns, “If you are not able to fully remove the base, they will come back more easily this way.”

If you are pulling weeds up by hand, De Foe recommends pulling them up after a good rain, when the ground is soft. It will make the task much easier, and it helps you grab the whole weed, including the root.

But what if this all sounds like hard work and you want an easier solution? "Using a weed killer isn’t the end of the world; just make sure to research the product, and keep in mind if you have kids or pets running around,” says De Foe.

Avoid sharp toolsI own various weed-removal tools that I use to remove weeds from my lawn, pathways, and flowerbeds, and they are all fairly invasive. When it comes to gravel, though, I take extra care. The same sharp blade you might use to scrape weeds out of patio cracks can easily slice through the landscape fabric and encourage more weeds to break through.

Shift the debrisOne job that will prevent weeds from growing in your gravel is to keep the area tidy and remove any debris — especially in the fall when fallen leaves or pine needles build up quickly. “It will save you a lot of time down the road, and those leaves can become a new base for weeds to grow if left alone for an extended period of time,” she adds.

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Going back to a screen after the Fitbit Air was jarring. Here’s what the Fitbit Edge gets right and wrong

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

So you’re trying to pick between the $99 Fitbit Air and the $179 Fitbit Edge. Both have a lot in common — they share the same heart rate sensor, charger, and Google Health app ecosystem. But there are also a lot of differences between the two new trackers. I’ve been wearing the Fitbit Air since it launched in May 2026, and I’ve recently taken it off my wrist to test the new Fitbit Edge. Read on to find out what I liked and disliked.

If you’re looking to read reviews of both trackers before Black Friday, check out our Fitbit Air review as well as our Fitbit Edge review here on Tom’s Guide.

With no screen, buttons, or alerts to distract you — plus nearly a week of battery — the Fitbit Air is as easy-going as it is affordable. It’s also one of the best fitness trackers of the year and our overall favorite tracker for most Fitbit fans.

The Fitbit Edge is the perfect successor to the Fitbit Charge 6. It sports a bigger/brighter display, easier-to-use controls, more accurate elevation tracking, access to Google's latest health and safety features, and better battery performance. In our Fitbit Edge review, we said it offers just the right amount of fitness tracker for most folks.

If you’re into running, walking, or cycling, the choice is an obvious one — for $80 more than the Fitbit Air, you’re definitely getting a better fitness tracker with the Fitbit Edge. It has built-in GPS, which means you can leave your phone at home, and a 1.34-inch AMOLED display, which allows you to see live feedback as you move.

The Fitbit Edge also has an altimeter, which tracks your elevation during workouts and how many stairs you’ve climbed during the day, and an ECG monitor.

Despite being bigger and heavier than the Fitbit Air, the Fitbit Edge still does a good job of disappearing on the wrist. It’s dainty, and Google has released a huge range of swappable straps to suit every style. If you want a fitness tracker that’ll disappear, this isn’t quite as tiny as the Fitbit Air, but it still ticks that box.

I’ve used a lot of these AI-powered health coaches, and the Gemini-powered Google Health Coach is the best one I’ve tested. Rather than regurgitating your workout back to you, it offers actionable advice on how you should be training and recovering from your efforts. This applies to both devices, but you get real-time notifications on the Fitbit Edge, rather than having to log into the app to see your data.

At 32g and 11.58mm thick, the Fitbit Edge is by no means bulky on the wrist, especially compared to the likes of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 I’m normally wearing. That said, compared to the Fitbit Air, it’s still not as comfortable to wear overnight. One of the main selling points of the Fitbit Air is its ultra-light design. It weighs in at 12g, and the textile band is fast-drying, so unlike others on the market (cough, Garmin Cirqa) you won’t be left with a soggy wrist after showering, swimming, or washing the dishes.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There’s a reason why screenless trackers seem to be a growing trend: once you lose the non-stop buzzing on your wrist, it’s really hard to go back. Again, the Google ecosystem and the fact that these two Fitbits share a charger allows you to swap between the two, but if you’re looking for health, recovery, and sleep tracking and already own a regular watch, the Fitbit Air is the obvious choice.

It’s also worth noting here that, from a health perspective, you’re getting the same experience with the Fitbit Air, and it’s nearly half the price.

Fitbit promises seven days of battery life on both devices, and while I found that to be true with the Fitbit Air, no matter how many workouts I did, it was a different story with the Fitbit Edge.

Of course, this is largely down to the built-in GPS. Out of the box, the GPS on the device is automatically set to dynamic, which means it switches between using your phone’s GPS and the built-in GPS. When you switch the tracker to using the built-in GPS, I found it takes a hit on battery life, using around 11% for an hour-long run, and it didn’t last a full week.

When you switch the tracker to using the built-in GPS, I found it takes a hit on battery life, using around 11% for an hour-long run

That said, for most casual runners, dynamic GPS is more than enough, and you’re probably not clocking hour-long workouts every day.

As I’ve mentioned before, I’m frustrated by how little the Fitbit Edge’s button actually does. Sure, I love a physical button on a fitness tracker, but I’m not sure why Google didn’t give the Fitbit Edge’s button more functionality.

For example, you’d expect the button to start a run, not just stop it; instead, you still need to tap the screen before you start moving. Any runner knows nothing’s more frustrating than trying to swipe a touchscreen with sweaty fingers, especially on the start or finish line of a race.

#3467. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

This article appears in the December 2026 print issue

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

One 'Hunger Games' movie stands above the rest

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We’ve come a long way since Katniss Everdeen volunteered as tribute in “The Hunger Games.” It’s been almost 15 years since Jennifer Lawrence delivered that line and became an iconic action heroine. “The Hunger Games” brought the young adult genre to new heights and proved that these movies could be legitimate blockbusters by every measure.

After four flagship movies and one prequel, the franchise heads back to the past again in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.” The prequel revisits Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada) as a teenager competing in the 50th Hunger Games. Where does Haymitch’s outing rank among the franchise’s best movies? Let’s get into the rankings.

By the time “The Hunger Games” reached its conclusion, the franchise had run out of gas. After saving a brainwashed Peeta (Josh Hutcherson), President Coin (Julianne Moore) tasks Katniss and her band of rebels with liberating District 2 before retaking the Capitol. It's the final push to overthrow President Snow, but as Katniss pursues revenge, she begins to question the rebellion’s true intentions.

“The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2” isn’t necessarily a bad movie. The familiar group-on-one-last-mission trope builds to an exciting conclusion. However, it’s more concerned with reaching the finish line than saying anything new.

Splitting “Mockingjay” into two parts made financial sense, as the two movies combined to gross over $1.4 billion worldwide. Story-wise, a 390-page novel doesn’t need more than four hours of screen time. Whenever you end a movie on an unresolved cliffhanger, more often than not, fans are going to reject it. Guess what? Many fans, myself included, rejected the ending of “Mockingjay – Part 1.”

After being rescued from the arena in “Catching Fire,” Katniss is taken to the secret underground city of District 13. There, President Coin convinces Katniss to live up to her mockingjay reputation and become the face of the rebellion. Katniss eventually agrees to Coin’s request because she wants to save Peeta, who is being held captive in the Capitol. It’s the first movie in the franchise without the chaos of the arena, so expect less action. However, “Mockingjay – Part 1” is the best political thriller of the bunch, as it emphasizes its anti-war and anti-fascist themes the best.

Coming after the success of the four “Hunger Games” movies, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” had low odds of achieving success, though not as low as some of the tributes entering the arena. A new cast meant the absence of Lawrence, Hutcherson, Hemsworth, and the rest of the original ensemble. Second, it’s a prequel set before the days of Katniss Everdeen. Most importantly, it’s a story about a young President Snow — yes, the same tyrannical dictator who would rule Panem for decades. How are audiences supposed to sympathize with and grow attached to the future villain of the main trilogy?

That’s the best trick “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes” pulls off: no sympathy for Snow. You don’t feel sorry for him. Instead, it explores how trauma and grief can send a man down a path where embracing evil seems preferable to enduring hardship.

In the film, a young Coriolanus "Coryo" Snow (Tom Blyth) mentors District 12’s Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler) in the 10th Hunger Games. It’s the most grounded arena battle in the franchise, and the violence feels worse than ever before. It’s a fascinating origin story that had no business being this effective.

“The Hunger Games” is known for having a deep bench of talented supporting actors. Woody Harrelson famously played Haymitch Abernathy, a former winner of the Games who mentored Katniss and Peeta in District 12. Haymitch was first introduced as a drunk and despondent former victor who wanted nothing to do with the Hunger Games. As the movies progressed, viewers learned that Haymitch was one of the rebellion’s allies and had been for a long time.

Why was Haymitch depressed all those years? “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” fills in the blanks, as it revisits Haymitch’s win in the 50th Hunger Games, the second Quarter Quell. Zada stars as the 16-year-old Haymitch, who is much happier thanks to the love of his family and girlfriend, Lenora Dove Baird (Whitney Peak).

After witnessing the Capitol’s hostility, Haymitch becomes the key figure in a plot to sabotage the Games once and for all. It’s a tad too long, but this movie soars because of Zada, who injects so much life and passion into his portrayal of Haymitch. It’s a true movie-star-in-the-making performance. Don’t be surprised if Marvel or DC is calling Zada to put on a cape in a few years.

The movie that kicked off the young adult dystopian movie wave was 2012’s “The Hunger Games.” On the day of the reaping, Katniss volunteers to take her younger sister’s place in the 74th Hunger Games. Katniss and Peeta, her fellow District 12 tribute, enter the arena with little hope of surviving. As the Games progress, Katniss reluctantly becomes a symbol of hope, and her defiance lays the foundation for a rebellion.

“The Hunger Games” was revolutionary for its time. It proved a young adult action franchise could be a profitable endeavor ($695 million worldwide). Lawrence became a legitimate star and rose to A-list status, which she maintains in 2026. The movie depicts a battle to the death, but its messages about authoritarianism, exploitation, and inequality are very sophisticated for a teen drama. Plus, it breaks an unwritten Hollywood rule—don’t kill kids. I commend the film for having the guts to show Rue’s death. Throw your 3s in the air!

There was only one answer. I consider myself a “real fan” of “The Hunger Games,” and real ones know that “Catching Fire” is the best book and movie in the franchise. It’s the best action movie of the bunch, with the most innovative arena, a top-notch supporting cast, and riveting twists. After Katniss and Peeta defy the Capitol, President Snow makes the duo parade around the districts to eliminate civil unrest.

When that doesn’t work, Snow announces a twist for the 75th Hunger Games: All tributes will be former winners. In other words, it’s back to the arena for Katniss and Peeta. “Catching Fire” has by far the best in-arena sequences, with my favorite scene being the opening of the Games, where Katniss teams up with her new ally (Finnick) to save Peeta. Forget the young adult genre; “Catching Fire” is an excellent action movie that improves upon its predecessor in nearly every way.

#3461. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

#3459. Jensen Huang says he’s ready to rejoin Nvidia as CEO (if asked)

Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO shook up the AI market and US economy last week, but now via The Wall Street Journal Huang has spoken out publicly for the first time since stepping down, and he signals he’s ready to return as CEO if asked.

Today Robbie Whelan at The Wall Street Journal published Jensen Huang’s first public statement since departing Nvidia last week.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a short statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

To be clear, I’m also willing to step in as CEO of Nvidia if asked. I’ve owned several generations of their graphics cards, so I have plenty of experience with their products. More importantly, this is probably my best chance of finally having enough cash to afford a Mac with 32GB of RAM.

The timing is likely no coincidence, as Nvidia is set to report its quarterly earnings later today.

Even though Huang technically resigned as CEO rather than being fired, it was clear that his ouster wasn’t exactly his choice. Thus, today’s statement is the former CEO formally putting it out into the world that he’s ready to return if asked.

Since Huang stepped down, President Trump publicly called on Apple’s Tim Cook to step in as Nvidia CEO. But it’s expected that a new CEO—assuming it’s not Huang—will take much longer for the company to find and Cook is unlikely to want the job.

What do you make of Huang’s remarks today? Let us know in the comments.

Here's how to enhance your GTA 6 experience on PS5

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 is finally here! It’s easily Rockstar Games’ most ambitious title ever, featuring dense environments and lush soundscapes. You get a rich visual and audio experience out of the box, but tweaking a few PS5 settings can enhance it.

We’re talking specifically about the PS5’s settings, since GTA 6 has no graphical settings beyond a motion blur slider. Even on a PS5 Pro, your options are limited. But with a few smart tweaks, you can make GTA 6 look and sound its best on either PS5 console.

Here are the 3 PS5 settings you need to check to enhance your GTA 6 experience.

This one is for folks who own an OLED TV. In the Video Output tab in System Settings, scroll down to HDR. Click it, and you’ll be taken to another screen to calibrate the console’s HDR.

You’ll adjust the brightness across three pages. On the first two pages, press up or down until the sun logo disappears. On the last page, dial it all the way down, since your OLED TV can display deep blacks.

GTA 6 also has in-game HDR calibration. Just follow the on-screen prompts to get your desired result, though I’ve found the default settings work well.

After 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto VI has arrived. Set in the state of Leonida, with Vice City at its heart, you play Jason and Lucia, two criminals forced into an increasingly dangerous situation as they seek their fortune, discovering the darker side of the sunniest spot in America.

GTA 6 is undoubtedly a feast for the eyes, but you shouldn’t neglect the audio side of the equation.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

While the PS5 didn’t launch with Dolby Atmos, it now supports the feature. So if you have a soundbar or surround sound system that supports Dolby Atmos, you should definitely enable it. To do so, go to Sound in System Settings, click Sound Output, scroll down to Audio Format, and select Dolby Atmos.

GTA 6 targets 30 frames per second on all consoles. Rockstar Games even confirmed to Kotaku that the PS5 Pro won’t be patched to run at 40 or 60 fps. That said, we can’t completely rule it out.

If GTA 6 ever adds a performance-enhancing feature, you’ll want to set the PS5 Pro for that. In the Video Output tab of the Screen and Audio settings, make sure that VRR is set to Automatic for unsupported games and that 120Hz output is set to Automatic.

Again, this won’t make GTA 6 run at a higher frame rate, but it prepares your PS5 Pro if it ever does. As a rule of thumb, you should have these settings enabled anyway, since many PlayStation titles offer 40 fps modes.

Until we get the inevitable PC version of GTA 6, we'll have to make do with the experience on existing consoles, in this case, the PS5. That said, the advice I've given you should help you get the most from the game. Have fun in Vice City!

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt cordless 20-volt cutout saw is on sale on Amazon for $102.95, 53% off its typical price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a 20-volt DeWalt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for custom trimming drywall, cutting custom shapes for going around outlet covers, or custom cutting trim in tight spaces.

The DeWalt 20-volt cordless angle grinder is on sale at Lowe’s for $209, 47% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a 4-amp-hour battery, but you’ll need a DeWalt 20-volt charger to use it. This is a good tool for metalworking or for grinding down screw tips that poke through or trimming bolt ends off.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. For most home tool sets, Ryobi is a solid, durable, and versatile brand. If you plan to use your tools occasionally for home maintenance, this is the best bang for your buck. #3454. Fiona the Hippo's Necropsy Results Revealed After Her Death

Fiona the Hippo's necropsy results found that no effort to save the animal would have worked after the beloved hippopotamus swallowed a knit hat.

The Cincinnati Zoo shared Friday that her necropsy showed the hat had been lodged in the middle of her small intestine for days before she died.

To put that in perspective, the piece of clothing was located about 50 feet from the end of her intestines.

Cincinnati Zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger, said ... "Upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object. The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible. No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked."

We reported earlier ... Fiona ate the hat last week after a child threw it into the enclosure. In a freak accident, the hat managed to hit a fan and slip past a gap to find its way into Fiona's habitat.

Unfortunately, vets who tried to remove it were unsuccessful.

#3452. IEEE Program Schools Preuniversity Educators On Tech Topics

The TryEngineering workshops help teachers deliver engaging STEM lessons

An educator constructs a microchip model during the IEEE Making a Microchip lesson plan demonstration.

Now in their third year, the IEEE TryEngineering educator sessions continue to empower preuniversity teachers with specialized professional development programs on engineering topics and classroom-tested lessons.

This year’s sessions have focused on educating teachers about artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. Three sessions were held in the United States and one session was held in Egypt.

In all, 54 educators learned about the engineering design process this year. They received an overview of TryEngineering resources including the Making of a Microchip and Train Your Tree lesson plans.

Workshops are scheduled later this year in Greece and Guatemala.

The TryEngineering program is administered by IEEE Educational Activities.

These teachers and guest speakers attended the two-day session held at the Florida Semiconductor Institute and SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.IEEE Educational Activities

Central to the educator session program’s success is its university network. Host campuses welcome teachers into their facilities, where faculty provide background information about some of the technologies being taught, as well as possible engineering career paths and job opportunities for students.

This year’s sessions involved the educators in hands-on projects. Facilitators at each location were selected based on their experience in engineering education, and they worked with the TryEngineering staff on their presentations.

Sixteen teachers from nine schools participated in the session, held in Cairo. It was facilitated by Marwa Soudi, an IEEE member, and Senior Member Stamatis Dragoumanos, past chair of the IEEE preuniversity coordinating committee. GEMS provided outstanding STEM facilities for teachers, Soudi and Dragoumanos said. Participants received an overview of the Working With Wind Energy and Tall Tower Challenge lesson plans.

Another educator session is scheduled for later this year.

Educators from across the state gathered at the university’s Florida Semiconductor Institute, headquartered in Gainesville, and FSI’s NeoCity high-tech manufacturing campus near Orlando. The session was hosted by Roseanne Perez, an FSI workforce development program specialist, and Sophia Watson, FSI’s assistant director of workforce development. The two-day experience featured an inside look at microelectronics through a guided tour of a SkyWater Technology chip manufacturing facility.

Engineering instructor Mary Acken facilitated hands-on lesson demonstrations for the 15 attending teachers.

Reflecting on the workshop’s impact, one participant said the SkyWater tour was excellent, the instructors were great, and the teachers enjoyed learning from like-minded educators.

Michael Kozicki, an IEEE member, and Stefan Myhajlenko from the university’s engineering school welcomed 11 Arizona teachers to the Tempe campus.

The session was facilitated by Janet Hartkopf, an Arizona school leader and a former TryEngineering educator session participant. Hartkopf highlighted collaborative learning, the need for diverse perspectives in engineering education, and career paths.

The teachers received instruction on how to implement the hands-on lessons in their classrooms, and they toured the university’s NanoFab facility to observe microelectronics research.

“This training was amazing!” said a participant who leads an elementary after-school STEM club. “I loved the hands-on lessons and e-books, which I will definitely be using with my students. I am excited to explore all the resources on the TryEngineering website. The experts from ASU were great.”

Sixteen STEM educators attended this session, held at the university’s International Institute for Biosensing in Minneapolis. Its director, Patricia Khashayar, an IEEE member, introduced participants to the capabilities of the university’s Supercomputing Institute and Nano Center.

Under the guidance of Claire Dietz, an education and outreach coordinator, and Pam Schumacher, an instructor at St. Paul College, the teachers completed classroom-ready lessons including a photonics experiment using the Nano Center’s equipment. Schumacher attended last year’s TryEngineering educator session.

Nano Center Director Sarah Swisher, an IEEE senior member, provided an overview of semiconductor operations and highlighted growing job opportunities for the state’s young people.

The experience inspired all 16 teachers to plan student field trips to the Nano Center during the upcoming academic year, they said.

“Great class!” one participant said. “I’m excited to bring some of the TryEngineering materials back to our school.”

This year’s sessions built on the momentum from last year when, with financial support from Onsemi’s Giving Now program, nearly 80 teachers attended sessions across five U.S. states and Mexico.

Driven by that success and the demand for more, the IEEE Educational Activities Board continued its support. Upcoming global sessions are expected to expand the program’s international footprint.

“I appreciated the time to collaborate with peers on how to implement hands-on lessons,” one participating teacher this year said. Some participants said they planned follow-up visits with the experts and campus tours.

You can learn more about the sessions by emailing TryEngineering.

This article was updated on 18 November 2026.

Debra Gulick is director of IEEE student and academic educational programs.

#3451. VSCO launches its first native Mac photo editor with RAW support, batch editing, more

VSCO today released Studio Pro Desktop, its first native photo editor for Mac, bringing many of the company’s familiar editing tools to macOS, alongside new features aimed at photographers working with large numbers of images. Here are the details.

Professional and amateur photographers just got a new alternative for editing and managing their photos on Mac with the release of VSCO Studio Pro, a native macOS app that brings the company’s popular editing tools to the desktop for the first time.

More than that, VSCO Studio Pro integrates with the company’s broader ecosystem of photography tools, allowing users to manage their workflow from importing and editing photos to delivering finished images to clients through VSCO Galleries, without having to manually export and upload them to another app.

It also supports keyboard shortcuts similar to those found in other popular photo editors, making it easier for photographers familiar with those apps to get started.

Here’s Eric Wittman, CEO of VSCO, on today’s launch:

“Photographers deserve tools built around how they actually work. […] 75% of VSCO Pro members have used our presets in the last six months. Now those looks live on the desktop, with one connected workflow from camera to client delivery and nothing getting in the way.

The first thing users will notice, and then continue to notice when using VSCO Studio Pro, is how fast it is. From changing the grid size, to sorting images, to applying presets by rolling the cursor over each of the 200+ presets, pretty much everything about VSCO Studio Pro feels as real-time and instant as it can be when dealing with large numbers of images.

As for importing photos, VSCO Studio Pro supports Apple Photos, local folders, SD cards, and external drives, and offers RAW compatibility with more than 800 cameras from 20 brands. Users can also choose whether to work with files in their original location or copy them elsewhere.

Under the hood, VSCO Studio Pro Desktop combines Apple’s Core Image RAW processing with the company’s own Reflex image processing engine, which handles presets and editing adjustments.

Batch editing in VSCO Studio Pro Desktop can handle anywhere from two to 500 images at once, which is great for quickly applying the same preset or film-inspired look (including Kodak Portra, Kodachrome, Fujifilm Velvia, and Kodak Tri-X), or making adjustments to an entire set of photos simultaneously, with changes appearing across all selected images in real time.

And speaking of presets, VSCO Studio Pro packs an exclusive one called IOE1 Pro, developed with photographer Joe Greer. IOE1 Pro, as well as VSCO’s other presets, allow users to adjust the strength, color, tone, and contrast, further helping them fine-tune each look to their liking.

VSCO Studio Pro’s editing tools include the usual suspects photographers might expect from photo editing software, including exposure, contrast, fade, highlights, shadows, whites, blacks, skin tone, temperature, tint, hue, saturation, lightness, sharpening, clarity, vignetting, and grain adjustments for strength, size, and color.

VSCO is also working to expand its toolset to include bloom and halation effects, curves, masks, and a remove tool for users looking for more control over their edits and to make more precise, localized adjustments to their images.

Also in the works are new organizational features, including projects for managing groups of photos, as well as culling tools that will allow users to rate images with stars and mark them as accepted or rejected, making it easier to sort through large photo collections.

Once users are happy with their adjustments, they can export their photos individually or in batches, choosing the file name, format, resolution, and compression quality. VSCO Studio Pro also offers resizing presets for web, social media, and client delivery, as well as the option to save the finished images to a folder of their choice.

And speaking of client delivery, users can publish their edited photos directly to VSCO Galleries, allowing them to share full-resolution images without having to export them and upload them separately elsewhere.

VSCO Studio Pro Desktop is available today as a free download for Apple Silicon Macs, with full feature access requiring a VSCO Pro membership, starting at $4.99 per month or $59.99 per year, or a VSCO One membership. You can see it in action below:

To learn more about VSCO Studio Pro Desktop, follow this link.

Apple, Garmin, and Oura all appear in our guide to this year's best sleep trackers with the Oura Ring taking the top spot. In this sleep tracker triple header, I'm exploring the key differences between the Oura Ring 5 vs the Apple Watch vs the Garmin Index Sleep Monitor to help you decide which wearable to is worth your money in the Black Friday sales.

And if you're upgrading other aspects of your sleep set up too, then take a look at our guide to this year's best Black Friday mattress deals.

At MSRP, the Oura Ring 5 starts at $399 and goes up to $499, depending what shade (or "finish") you choose. For example, a silver Oura Ring 5 is $399, while a gold Oura Ring 5 is $499.

The 5 isn't the only Oura Ring discounted right now — the older Oura Ring 4 is now from just $249.99 (was $349.99) at Amazon. You can read my Oura Ring 5 vs Oura Ring 4 comparison guide to see if it's worth downgrading to save money.

But before you buy the new-and-improved Oura Ring 5, there are some hidden costs to consider. First, you need a sizing kit.

This is completely free direct from Oura, or $10 at Amazon. Second, the monthly subscription. Yes, you need to pay a $5.99 membership fee every month to use Oura's sleep tracking (the first month is free).
